Due dates

Lima-area owners pay twice a year. Installments land on the second Wednesday of February and again on the second Wednesday of July. The cycle for tax year 2026 (paid in 2027) is February 10 and July 14, 2027. Notices typically mail in January and June, though the treasurer cannot print them until the auditor delivers the calculated tax file, so the mailing date moves.

A house on county sewer should have that balance checked alongside the taxes, since the treasurer collects both.

Late payments and the postmark trap

State law sets the penalty at 5 percent for a payment postmarked in the 10 days after the due date, rising to 10 percent beyond that. If you think a penalty is unwarranted, send in an Application for Remission to request a waiver.

The treasurer warns about postmarks. The stamp typically records when postal machinery first scanned the envelope, possibly a day or more after you dropped it in the box. Because Ohio law reads that stamp, a check mailed near the deadline may count as late. Send it early, request a hand-canceled postmark at the counter, or pay in person, by card or by e-check.

How to pay the treasurer

Accepted forms of payment are cash, checks, cards and e-checks. Federal holidays are closed days. Visit the counter at 237 N Main St, Suite 123, Lima, OH 45801, or call (419) 223-8515. Closing time reads 4:30 p.m. on the home page and 4:15 p.m. in the FAQ, so phone ahead on deadline day.

  • Use the Search and Pay Property Taxes tab on the website, or dial 1-419-765-6401.
  • Hand it over at the counter or leave it in the drop box beside the automatic doors outside the courthouse.
  • Walk into a county branch of Superior Credit Union or The Union Bank Company. Non-customers pay nothing extra, but this works only from mid-January to the February deadline and from mid-June to the July deadline.
  • Card or e-check payments run through an outside vendor that adds 2.40 percent (minimum $2) for cards and a flat $1 for e-checks.

Two plans help if lump sums are hard. TEPP, an in-house escrow, divides the year's taxes into 10 months. AUTO-Pay pulls the exact amount from your bank on each due date, or in one draw each February.

How the bill is figured

Start with market value and take 35 percent to reach assessed value. Multiply that by the effective rate for your political subdivision for gross tax. A levy takes effect the year voters approve it, yet the matching bill arrives a year later, so a five-year levy passed in November first appears on the next year's bills.

The county auditor's site has a property search and a tax calculator. On the treasurer's side you will find rates, tax duplicates, and lists of school districts, cities and villages, and townships. Search your own parcel, since school district and village or township lines drive the rate.

Appealing your valuation

Owners who think the assessed value is too high file a Complaint Against Valuation with the county auditor, with a stated window of January 1 to March 31. Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 sets the outer limit at March 31 of the next year or the end of first-half collection, whichever comes later. Mailed complaints are dated by postal postmark, and a meter stamp from a private machine does not qualify.

  • Every complaint is sent on by the auditor to the board of revision.
  • A counter-complaint from another party is allowed within 30 days of notice.
  • An original complaint must be decided within 180 days of the last filing date.
  • Until it is decided, the treasurer takes tax computed on your claimed value.
  • Submit all your evidence to the board. Anything held back can be barred from use on appeal.

Storm, fire or other damage has its own form, the Application for Valuation Deduction. File as soon as possible, because refunds for prior years are not issued.

Tax reductions for homeowners

Homeowners usually meet three programs. A 2.5 percent rollback, the Owner Occupancy Credit, covers a primary residence. The Homestead reduction is open to owners 65 or older and to people permanently and totally disabled, applied for through the auditor (postmarks accepted). CAUV applies to commercial farmland valuation.

They show up again at sale time, because the buyer's statement of value under section 319.202 asks if the seller's taxes were reduced. Find out from the auditor what your parcel carries before you sign a contract.

Selling: who owes the tax

The tax goes with the owner, and closings usually prorate it. Proration is a closing-table job, not an auditor job, and if it gets skipped the new owner receives the bill. Taxes are charged on the parcel as it stood January 1, which means a lot divided mid-year is billed whole until a tax split is requested. The prior owner's name may stay in the treasurer's system for a year after transfer without changing who owes.

Transfer costs are a conveyance fee of $3.00 per thousand of price and a $.50 per parcel transfer charge, both normally listed by the title company.

One order that works: get balances from the treasurer for taxes and sewer, pass them to the closing agent, check the proration line on the statement, and hold on to your last payment receipts. If you are selling for cash, the same balance requests apply, though the sale can close faster because no lender is waiting on a payoff letter.

What to have ready at the treasurer's counter

Bring the parcel number from your last bill, or look it up on the auditor's site first. Ask for the current balance on the real estate account and, if you have sewer service, the sewer account. If you plan to pay on the spot, cash, checks, cards and e-checks all work at the office. Get a receipt. A seller who is closing soon should also ask whether any complaint is pending on the parcel, because that changes which amount the treasurer will accept while it is open.

Allen County housing numbers

Allen County has about 100,881 residents. Median household income is $64,038, median gross rent is $922, and monthly ownership costs run $1,240 with a mortgage and $535 without. To see what homes on your street are assessed at, use the auditor's property search.

Frequently asked questions

When is the second half of property tax due in Allen County?

Wednesday, July 14, 2027 for tax year 2026, after a first half due Wednesday, February 10, 2027.

What is the penalty for paying Allen County property tax late?

Five percent for a postmark within 10 days after the due date, then 10 percent. A remission application can request a waiver.

Can I pay Allen County property tax with a credit card?

Yes, online, by phone at 1-419-765-6401 or at the counter. Expect 2.40 percent (at least $2) on cards and $1 on an e-check.

How do I appeal my Allen County property value?

Send a Complaint Against Valuation to the county auditor by March 31 (the window opens January 1). The auditor routes it to the board of revision.

Who pays the property tax when I sell my Allen County home?

The tax goes with ownership and is typically prorated at closing. Ask the closing agent to settle the split on the statement.

Offices behind the tax bill

Jefferson houses the two offices you need. Values and value disputes are the auditor's, at the courthouse, 25 W Jefferson St, 440-576-3783. Billing and collecting are the treasurer's. Direct questions about a bill, a payoff for a sale, or a delinquent balance to the treasurer.

Ashtabula County fills Ohio's northeastern corner, with Jefferson as seat. In 2020 it had 97,574 residents and 46,237 housing units, 14.9% of them vacant. Owners lived in 71.0% of occupied homes.

Housing and taxing districts

The county covers 1,368 square miles, 49% of it Lake Erie water. Three cities (Ashtabula, Conneaut and Geneva) sit beside seven villages: Andover, Geneva-on-the-Lake, Jefferson, North Kingsville, Orwell, Roaming Shores and Rock Creek. Lake-effect snow falls often, so roofs, gutters and drainage matter to buyers.

A lakeside village house and an inland farmhouse can fall in quite different taxing districts. Keep the parcel number from your bill handy, since every question below starts there.

How to challenge your property value

The county's complaint season runs January 1 through March 31, with filings handed to the auditor for the Board of Revision. ORC 5715.19(A)(1) in fact stretches the deadline to March 31 of the following year or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later. Mail counts as filed on its postal postmark date, not a private meter date.

The Board changes values, never tax dollars, and you carry the burden of proof. Gather paperwork:

  • A closing statement and contract from a recent purchase.
  • An independent appraisal.
  • Contractor quotes for defects.
  • Rent rolls and expense records for a rental.

Two arguments get nowhere: how quickly your tax rose, and how a neighbor's parcel is valued. Deliver paper forms to the auditor, or e-file to bor@ashtabulacounty.gov. Call the Board at 440-576-1484 on weekdays between eight and half past four.

After you file

A certified letter announcing the hearing should arrive at least ten days early. The Board owes you a ruling within 180 days after the last day to file. An owner who disagrees has 30 days from the decision letter's postmark to appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals in Columbus or the Court of Common Pleas in Jefferson. File the notice of appeal with the Board of Revision as well as the forum you pick.

Two more rules from ORC 5715.19 affect timing:

  • Pending a decision, you may pay on your claimed value, and the treasurer must take it.
  • Should the final value exceed your claim, interest runs on the gap from the original due date.
  • Give the Board everything. Evidence withheld there may be barred on appeal.

Filing again next year

Not right away. After a complaint on a parcel, subsection (A)(2) blocks further complaints for the remainder of that interim period, unless something changed after the lien date. Qualifying changes are an arm's-length sale, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement, or a drop of at least fifteen percent in occupancy that hurts the property economically.

A school board or other party may answer a large request with a counter-complaint, and the threshold is $17,500 in taxable value.

A seller's order of operations

Begin with the auditor's parcel record: confirm year built and any additions, which buyers and lenders always ask about. Then call the treasurer for the current balance, remembering the second half if it is unpaid. Weigh a complaint before March 31. A lower value can ease a listing, and a pending case changes what you tender. Then set aside the transfer fee for closing and ask about a county transfer tax. Hand the title company all of it early so nothing surprises you at the table.

Preparing for a hearing

A good file is short and ties each paper to one claim. Lead with the strongest proof of market value, usually a recent closing statement or an independent appraisal. Add repair estimates if defects hold the value down, and rent and expense statements if the property earns income. Label each page, make a copy for the Board, and keep one for yourself. Since evidence you hold back can be shut out of a later appeal, put everything in at the first hearing rather than saving some for round two.

Plan for the clock as well. The hearing notice comes by certified mail, and the Board has 180 days from the last filing day to rule, so a complaint filed in March may still be open when you want to list. Tell your agent and the title company, and keep paying on your claimed value so nothing falls behind.

Dates and rules to know

Complaint windowJanuary 1 through March 31

Deed transfer fee$1 minimum, or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction, if higher

Those are the statewide baselines. The exact dates for your parcel are on your own bill or from the treasurer.

What the auditor charges on transfer

On a deed transfer the auditor collects the greater of $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value, with any fraction rounded up to a full $100 (ORC 319.54(G)(3)). Sellers pay. A Chapter 322 transfer tax, if the commissioners enacted one, is added, so check with the auditor.

The buyer files a value statement alongside. ORC 319.202 has that form record whether the seller had a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction or farm-use valuation, and farmland leaving the program can owe a recoupment charge. Spousal gifts, parent-to-child gifts and delinquent-tax sales are exempt.

Selling with taxes owed

Ask the treasurer for a payoff before you sign a sales contract. Unpaid taxes appear in the title search and normally come out of the seller's proceeds at closing. A pending value complaint should be mentioned to the title company, since the tender rule above may set the amount due.

Empty houses, roofs battered by lake-effect winters and parcels with back taxes can all sell as-is using the same payoff steps. Get the parcel record from the auditor first so acreage and building details agree with your deed.

A cash buyer leaves the sequence intact. The payoff, transfer fee and value statement still come first. What disappears is the lender's appraisal and underwriting, so timing depends mostly on how quickly the treasurer and auditor respond.

Frequently asked questions

When can I file a property value complaint in Ashtabula County?

The county's window is January 1 through March 31, though the statute allows a later cutoff when first-half collection closes after March 31. Mail is dated by postmark.

Which office answers questions about an Ashtabula County tax bill?

The treasurer answers for bills and payments. For values and exemptions, the auditor is at 440-576-3783, and the Board of Revision line is 440-576-1484.

Does the Board of Revision lower my tax bill?

Only indirectly. It changes the value, and the tax follows. Tax increases and neighbors' values are not arguments it will weigh.

Can I appeal a Board of Revision decision?

Yes. You have 30 days from the postmark on the decision letter to go to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals in Columbus or the Court of Common Pleas in Jefferson. Copy the Board of Revision on the notice.

How much is the auditor's transfer charge?

The greater of $1 or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction. The seller pays, plus any county transfer tax the auditor can confirm.

Who to call about Athens County property tax

Start with two offices. Values and exemption forms are the auditor's job, at 15 S. Court Street in Athens. Dial 740-592-3223 for the Real Estate Division. Bills and payments belong to the treasurer, who also handles delinquent payment plans, escrow plans and mobile home tax.

The treasurer also leads the county land bank, so an empty, run-down house with back taxes may attract that office as well as a buyer.

Housing around Athens

Athens County is hill country, 508 square miles of steep ridges and creek valleys drained mostly by the Hocking River. Athens is both the county seat and the largest community. The 2020 census found 62,431 people in 26,386 housing units, with 10.2% of units vacant and 45.6% of occupied homes rented.

So many sellers here are landlords with houses near campus. Landlords should confirm each parcel's owner-occupancy status at the auditor's office before listing.

Payment deadlines and penalties

Your bill carries the actual deadlines, so use the current one instead of last year's calendar. The statutory baseline in ORC 323.12 is December 31 for everything, or half by that date and the balance by June 20. A mailed payment counts as on time when the postmark is dated no later than the final day.

Ohio allows no grace period, so a late payment normally draws a penalty automatically. Mailed checks risk lateness because the Postal Service no longer postmarks on the day it takes the mail. Paying electronically adds $0.50. Owners who cannot pay everything at once can phone or visit the treasurer about a plan. Mobile home bills go out right after the regular bills with the same due date.

Why bills vary across the county

Land use here ranges from the university city to former coal and salt country to farm and forest. Which levies stack up on a parcel depends on its school district and township. Five school districts serve residents: Alexander Local, Athens City, Federal Hocking Local, Nelsonville-York City and Trimble Local.

A house in Athens and a similar one in Trimble can get different bills. The taxing district code on your parcel, available from the auditor, explains the gap.

The 2026 reappraisal

The county reappraises everything for tax year 2026. Values are set as of January 1, 2026 and first appear on bills payable in 2027. Owners are asked to review the posted figures for acreage, building size and construction details and phone the Real Estate Division about mistakes. Since the site shows the new value only, set it beside your second-half 2025 bill.

The auditor also summarizes several late-2025 state laws that limit automatic tax growth:

  • House Bill 186 creates an Inflation Cap Credit for some school districts hit by the 20-mill floor, itemized on the bill.
  • House Bill 335 limits growth in inside millage during valuation reset years to inflation.
  • House Bill 129 changes how the school district 20-mill floor is calculated, beginning with tax year 2026.

These laws do not eliminate property taxes, repeal voted levies, reduce school bond millage or freeze values.

Disputing a value

File the complaint with the auditor, who sends it to the Board of Revision, where the treasurer holds a seat. You have until the end of March of the next tax year, or the close of first-half collection when that comes later (ORC 5715.19(A)(1)).

Notice of the hearing must reach the parties ten days in advance, and a decision is due within 180 days of the last filing day. Meanwhile you may pay on your claimed value, which the treasurer has to take. Interest accrues on any shortfall if the final value is higher. Refiling in the same interim period takes a new event: an arm's-length sale, casualty loss, a major improvement or a fifteen percent swing in occupancy.

Seller's plan

First pull the auditor's parcel record and check acreage, building size and year built, which a buyer's lender will also review. Second, learn whether the parcel carries a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, since transfer paperwork asks. Third, request a payoff and any payment plan balance from the treasurer. With a complaint pending, tell the title company so the amount due is worked out correctly. Last, budget for the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, both charged to the seller.

Timing a sale around the reappraisal

Because new values reach bills payable in 2027, a buyer shopping now may see a tax figure that is about to change. Look at the posted value for your parcel, compare it with the second-half 2025 bill, and be ready to explain the difference. If the new value looks wrong, the Real Estate Division at 740-592-3223 is the first call, and a formal complaint to the Board of Revision is the next step. Having the auditor's record corrected before you list saves arguments later in escrow.

The state laws listed above cap some of the automatic growth, so the bill may rise less than the value does. They do not freeze anything, and a seller should not promise a buyer a particular tax amount.

The income cap shown is for tax year 2024, so ask the auditor for the current limit.

What sellers handle at closing

Get a payoff from the treasurer and see whether a payment plan balance is open. At transfer the buyer files a value statement with the auditor under ORC 319.202, noting the seller's answers on homestead or owner-occupancy reductions and CAUV status. Land leaving CAUV can trigger a recoupment charge.

The auditor's conveyance fee under ORC 319.54(G)(3) is $1, or 10 cents per $100 of value or fraction if that is more. The seller pays it plus any Chapter 322 county transfer tax, so ask whether Athens County levies one.

Inherited, tenant-occupied and fixer-upper houses can all close as-is with these same steps. A cash buyer removes the lender but not the payoff, the value statement or the fee. Get the treasurer's payoff first so you know what leaves your proceeds.

Frequently asked questions

When are Athens County real estate taxes due?

Look at your bill for the dates. The statutory baseline is December 31, or half by then and the remainder by June 20, with no grace period.

Does the Athens County treasurer offer payment plans?

Yes, ask by phone or in person at the treasurer's office. Electronic payment adds $0.50.

When does the new Athens County reappraisal show up on my bill?

On bills payable in 2027, based on January 1, 2026 values.

Who qualifies for the Athens County homestead exemption?

People 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, living in the home on January 1, under an income cap for new applicants. Applications go to the auditor by December 31.

When does the window to contest a valuation close?

End of March of the next tax year, unless first-half collection closes later. The auditor takes the complaint and forwards it to the Board of Revision.

Belmont County housing market

Belmont County runs along Ohio's eastern border, with the Ohio River separating it from West Virginia. St. Clairsville is the county seat and Martins Ferry is the largest city. The county is part of the Wheeling metropolitan area.

The 2020 census counted 66,497 people, and the 2025 estimate is 64,434, which is 3.1 percent lower. The market is modest and owner-heavy. A typical owner-occupied home is worth $154,900, and 73.6 percent of its 27,195 households own. Median gross rent is $793 a month. Almost 25 percent of residents are 65 or older, which bears on the homestead credit discussed below. The auditor's records list 76,512 parcels.

Which offices handle property tax

A seller can finish every step inside the courthouse at 101 West Main Street, St. Clairsville. One office sets the value, one sends the bill, and one files the deed.

  • Auditor. Sets values, takes board of revision complaints and endorses deeds. The main line is 740-699-2130, real estate is 740-699-2132, and the deed transfer desk is 740-699-2136. Walk-in service runs weekdays, 8:30 to 4:30.
  • Treasurer. Mails the bills and takes payment. Phone 740-699-2145 on weekdays, 8:30 to 4:30.
  • Recorder. Files deeds and mortgages and looks after more than 220 years of county land records. The office does not run title searches.

Ask the treasurer for the tax rate in your district, which varies with the school and village levies, and for the balance on a given parcel number.

Due dates and the tax calendar

Real estate tax comes in two installments, mailed in January and June. The due dates usually fall in the third week of February and the third week of July, unless the bill says otherwise. Ohio bills taxes one year behind, so a bill arriving in 2026 covers tax year 2025.

Late payments and delinquent tax

The county adds a penalty first and interest later. Under Ohio Revised Code 323.121, a ten percent penalty attaches to an unpaid half, and interest on older delinquent tax runs at the rate set under section 5703.47.

Two points are blunt. A missing bill is no excuse, since the owner is responsible under section 323.13. A request to remit the penalty can still be filed when something outside the owner's control got in the way, such as hospitalization, a prolonged illness or the death of an immediate family member.

If you are behind, call 740-699-2145 and ask about payment options. The statute recognizes delinquent tax contracts, and while one stays in effect no ten percent penalty is added to the covered first-half taxes after the second-half collection period.

If back taxes go unpaid long enough, the parcel can reach tax foreclosure. The auditor's office has run forfeited land sales for parcels that failed to sell at foreclosure. The opening bid equals current taxes plus court costs, and the winning bidder pays the deed, conveyance and recording fees. Selling the house before that point keeps the proceeds with you.

Challenging your valuation

A valuation complaint is filed at the auditor's office. Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 allows owners until the later of the last day of March following the tax year or the day first-half collection closes. Plan on March 31.

The hearing notice must reach you at least ten days beforehand. A mailed complaint is judged by its United States postmark, and a private meter mark does not count. Taxing bodies such as a school board can file their own complaints or counter-complaints, so the district may appear at the hearing.

The most recent countywide reappraisal covered tax year 2024. Data mailers went to every property with a dwelling, owners could request informal reviews, and bills with the new values were mailed in January 2025, with the complaint window running January 1 to March 31, 2025.

Ohio generally limits an owner to one complaint per interim period, with listed exceptions such as an improvement added to the property or a 15 percent swing in occupancy. Ask the auditor which year Belmont County sits in before filing.

Homestead exemption and other breaks

The homestead exemption is the main one. The Ohio Department of Taxation publishes the tax year 2026 table: $29,700 of market value shielded for low-income seniors and disabled owners, $59,400 for disabled veteran owners, and a $41,000 income limit on the first group.

Send the application to the auditor before the year ends, because the credit is tied to the calendar year. A denied application can go to the board of revision on form DTE 106B, filed within 60 days of the notice. The treasurer's site also carries the homestead application for seniors, disabled residents and surviving spouses.

The credit does not pass with the deed, so the buyer qualifies on his or her own. That is why the deed paperwork asks about it.

Selling: how tax is handled at transfer

The auditor's endorsement is the first step on a deed. Section 319.202 has the buyer or a representative file a statement of value. That filing must say the seller was asked about any homestead or owner-occupancy tax cut on the house. If the seller answered yes, a sworn estimate of the cut is attached.

The auditor's fee comes from section 319.54(G)(3): a flat dollar or ten cents per hundred, whichever is higher. The same section lists exempt transfers, among them gifts within a family. Section 322.02 also lets a county levy a deed transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100. Call the deed transfer desk at 740-699-2136 for Belmont County's current conveyance rate.

If you still get a bill after closing, review the closing papers and then contact the title company, banker or agent. Unpaid tax that the closing statement never addressed can stay with the owner, so pay off or prorate the bill at the table. A cash buyer does not change that rule.

Frequently asked questions

Does Belmont County collect the second half in July?

Yes. Expect the second half around the third week of July, with the first half in the third week of February. Bills are mailed in January and in June or early July, and the printed date on your bill controls.

Who values a house in Belmont County?

The county auditor values every parcel. The treasurer only bills and collects. Complaints about value are filed with the auditor, whose office serves as the board's secretary.

How steep is the Belmont County late penalty?

A payment inside the ten-day grace window draws 5 percent. After that the penalty is 10 percent of what is still owed for the current year, and interest is added on older delinquent tax. A penalty remission request is possible for circumstances beyond your control.

Can I sell a Belmont County house with back taxes?

Yes. Phone 740-699-2145 for the payoff number, and the title company can pay it off at closing. Selling ahead of any tax foreclosure keeps the decision with you, where a forfeited land sale ends it.

Can the buyer keep my homestead reduction?

No. The credit belongs to the qualifying owner who lives in the home, and a buyer who qualifies must apply separately. Applications go to the auditor, with a December 31 cutoff.

Sixteen school districts, including Lakota, Fairfield, Hamilton, Middletown and Talawanda, reach into the county, which means your bill turns on the taxing districts your parcel sits in.

The 2026 reappraisal

The math begins with fair market value as the auditor sets it. Thirty-five percent of that is your taxable value. Run it against the combined mill rate per 1,000, tack on levies and special assessments, and credits come off at the end.

  • Parcel numbers. A real estate parcel is a letter followed by 13 numbers, and about 160,000 parcels exist in the county.

Because Ohio bills in arrears, a payment made in 2026 covers tax year 2025. Section 323.121 sets the late charge: 5 percent when full payment lands within the first ten days after the due date, and 10 percent after that.

Selling with taxes owed

A cash buyer follows the same payoff routine but can close quickly, with no lender appraisal or underwriting to wait on. Can I appeal my Butler County valuation every year?

Usually not. State law lets an owner file once per three-year valuation period, with a few listed exceptions. Use DTE Form 1 between January 1 and March 31.

$3.00 for every thousand of price, rounded up to the next hundred, plus $.50 per parcel. Make the check out to the Butler County Auditor. For exempt transfers that need Form 100EX, call 513-887-3154.

Two pages or fewer costs $39.00, and that already folds in the $5.00 preservation surcharge. Pages beyond that are $8.00 each, and a document with a layout problem picks up $20.00. Questions go to (513) 887-3192.

How the county values a house

The auditor sets fair market value and bills on 35% of it. Nearly 95,000 parcels sit in the county. A full reappraisal runs every six years, a midpoint update lands in between, and new construction is picked up annually.

Why second-half bills were delayed

Owners were told they could pay first-half taxes alone, with overpayments refunded after several weeks, and lenders were asked to hold their escrow payments. For a seller the practical lesson is to get a payoff figure that reflects the credits instead of reusing last year's second-half amount.

Who sends the Columbiana County tax bill

The county auditor, at 105 S. Market Street in Lisbon, sets values and takes deeds for transfer. The phone is 330-424-9515. The treasurer collects the tax and answers at 330-424-9514, and cash is taken at the counter between eight and four on weekdays. The recorder, at 330-424-9517, files the deed after the auditor has processed it.

Columbiana County sits on Ohio's eastern edge with Pennsylvania on its east line, and it covers about 534 square miles in eighteen townships. Lisbon is the seat and Salem is the largest city. Salem, Wellsville, East Palestine, Columbiana and East Liverpool are other places a seller might name on a deed.

Due dates, penalties and payment

Bills go out twice a year, usually in January and July, and Ohio bills a year behind. The treasurer's home page lists tentative 2027 dates of March 5 for first-half 2026 taxes and July 30 for second-half 2026 taxes. Confirm them with the office before closing a sale in either window.

Mail postmarked on the due date or earlier counts as on time. Payments made within ten days after the due date carry a 5% penalty and later ones 10%, under section 323.121, which waives half the penalty when full payment arrives inside ten days. Delinquent accounts add interest at a rate the Ohio Tax Commissioner sets each year.

  • Cash, checks, money orders and cashier's checks are taken at the counter. Do not mail cash.
  • Online payment runs through a provider that charges 2.95% on cards with a $2.00 minimum, 2.50% per transaction on ACH, and 2.95% plus $0.95 for a card payment by phone.
  • For a paid receipt by mail, return the whole bill with a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

How the county values property

Every six years the auditor hires a professional appraisal firm to set market value. Between those, the Ohio Department of Taxation looks at sales and economic factors every three years, and the auditor adjusts values to match. A higher value after a reappraisal does not guarantee a higher bill, because voters decide levies.

County government collects almost nothing from real estate tax. It takes only a 0.2 mill for debt retirement, after the commissioners chose to waive a 2 mill levy and rely on sales tax. A bill in Salem or Lisbon is therefore made up mostly of school, township, city or village, library and voted special levies.

If a mortgage servicer pays your tax from escrow, tell the treasurer in writing when the loan is paid off or refinanced, since a lender must notify the office of changes in writing. If you should have received a bill and did not, call at once.

Challenging a valuation

An owner who thinks a valuation is wrong can go to the county Board of Revision, the Ohio Department of Taxation, or Common Pleas Court. A Board of Revision complaint is due by March 31 and is processed through the auditor's office at 330-424-9515. Section 5715.19 can allow a later cutoff when first-half collection closes after March 31.

A late-fee complaint is a separate paper. The treasurer's office handles requests to remove a penalty, so call 330-424-9514 for the form and write down why the late charge should not apply.

Credits and special valuations

Four programs can lower a bill, and the auditor takes every application.

  • 10% rollback: a long-standing reduction for residential real estate not used in a business.
  • 2.5% rollback: for a homestead, meaning the dwelling plus up to one acre, with an application certifying primary residence.
  • Homestead exemption: for homeowners 65 or older and those permanently and totally disabled, for a dwelling and up to one acre. Ask the auditor for the current income limit and filing window.
  • Current agricultural use value: land with ten acres in commercial farming, or fewer than ten acres averaging at least $2,500 of yearly gross farm income, after three years of qualifying use. When land leaves the program, a charge equal to the extra tax over the previous three years applies.

Timber land run under state forestry rules may be taxed at half the local rate. A buyer taking over farm acreage should find out whether the parcel is enrolled before agreeing on a price.

Nearly one resident in four is 65 or older, so Homestead and the 2.5% rollback matter to many owners.

Steps for a Columbiana County sale

Start by calling the treasurer for the parcel's balance, including any contract payments still owed, so the title company can clear it from your proceeds. Next, confirm with the auditor which credits are on the parcel. If you held the owner-occupancy or homestead reduction, or the land is enrolled in the agricultural use program, the value statement will ask about it, and a farm parcel can trigger a recoupment charge when it leaves the program. Then the signed deed goes to the auditor first, where the conveyance fee is paid, and to the recorder second. If the lender is paid off at closing, make sure it records its release so the tax and deed records match. Sellers of an inherited house should ask the title agent which papers prove authority to sign.

Selling with taxes owed

A delinquent owner can set up a five-pay contract at the treasurer's office. The delinquent amount is split into five equal installments over two and a half years, and current taxes must still be paid on time throughout. Missing an installment voids the contract and foreclosure continues.

Section 323.121 stops penalty and interest while a valid contract stays in effect, so a sale can close with the contract balance paid at the table. Request the parcel's payoff from the treasurer and let the title company re-verify it shortly before closing. A cash buyer can close sooner, but the same payoff and deed steps apply.

A deed in this county goes to the auditor on the state's DTE 100 conveyance form before it reaches the recorder. The recorder's fees follow Revised Code sections 317.32 and 317.36, which split the basic fee equally between the recording fee and the Ohio Housing Trust Fund, with an optional county preservation charge on top.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Columbiana County?

The county treasurer, at 105 South Market Street in Lisbon, phone 330-424-9514. The auditor at 330-424-9515 values property and takes applications for credits.

When are Columbiana County second-half 2026 taxes due?

Tentatively July 30, 2027, with first-half 2026 taxes tentatively due March 5, 2027. Confirm both with the treasurer before relying on them.

What late fee does Columbiana County charge?

A 5% penalty for payments made within ten days after the due date and 10% after that. Interest is added on delinquent accounts at a rate the Ohio Tax Commissioner sets.

Can I pay a delinquent Columbiana County bill in installments?

Yes. A five-pay contract divides the delinquency into five equal installments over about two and a half years. Current taxes must stay paid, and one missed installment voids the contract.

How do I dispute a Columbiana County property value?

File a complaint with the Board of Revision by March 31 through the auditor's office. Appeals can also go to the Ohio Department of Taxation or Common Pleas Court.

At sale, the seller covers the conveyance fee from ORC 319.54: $1 or ten cents per hundred dollars of value, whichever is larger. Property tax here is a two-office job. The auditor sets each parcel's worth, and the treasurer converts it into a bill and takes payment. You will find both in the Darke County Courthouse at 504 S. Broadway, Greenville, from eight to four on weekdays.

The auditor also runs the county real estate website, which has a parcel search, a map, a sales report, a delinquency report, a tax estimator and a conveyance fee calculator. The downloadable forms mentioned below live there too.

Farm country and what it means for a sale

Darke is a farm county on the Indiana border, and Greenville is its seat and only city. The 2020 count placed 71.7 percent of residents in rural areas across roughly 600 square miles. It also tallied 22,599 housing units, with 7.4 percent vacant, and owners occupied about three in four of the homes in use.

Many sellers here hold acreage, outbuildings or a house on a split-off lot, and each of those touches its own tax rule. Farmland may carry an agricultural valuation, a split changes the parcel record, and a country house can fall in a school district other than the one its mailing address implies.

How often the auditor revalues homes

Every six years the auditor conducts a general reappraisal, with an update three years after each. In the years between, a value moves only for new building, demolition, a lot split or a Board of Revision order.

Tax rates differ by taxing district, and the auditor's forms page lists rates by year going back to 2009. The same house value therefore produces a different bill inside Greenville than in a village school district. Try the tax estimator, then ask the real estate division which district your parcel belongs to.

When Darke County tax is due

ORC 323.12 allows two routes. You can pay the full year by December 31, or pay a first half by that day and a second half by June 20. A check that arrives late still counts if the envelope carries a Postal Service postmark from the due date or earlier. A mark from a private postage meter does not qualify.

The treasurer may leave the books open a little longer for a collection period, so go by the dates on your own bill. The real estate website has a tax payment cart for paying online.

  • If a lender escrows your tax, tell it you hold a copy of the bill.
  • Behind on tax? Look at the delinquency report on the auditor's site and ask the treasurer for a payoff number ahead of listing.

How to dispute a Darke County value

Start with state form DTE 1, which goes to the auditor and then to the Board of Revision. ORC 5715.19 sets March 31 of the following tax year as the limit, pushed out to the end of first-half collection if that comes later.

The auditor's forms page has the DTE 1, the board's rules of practice, and a second form, DTE 2, for complaints about something other than market value. A few statutory rules affect sellers:

  • State the dollar amount by which you say the value is wrong.
  • You may pay tax on the claimed value while the matter is pending, though a final value above that figure brings interest on the gap.
  • Refiling in the same reappraisal period requires a change since your last complaint, for instance a sale between unrelated parties, a casualty loss or a major improvement.
  • The board owes a ruling within 180 days of the filing deadline, after notifying you of the hearing at least ten days in advance.
  • Give the board every piece of evidence you have, since withheld evidence can be barred on appeal.

Homestead, owner-occupancy and farmland breaks

Three programs come up most often: the homestead credit, the owner-occupied residence reduction, and farmland valuation at current agricultural use. Each has its own application on the auditor's forms page.

Three routes qualify an owner for the homestead credit: reaching age 65 by December 31 of the filing year, being permanently and totally disabled as of January 1, or being a surviving spouse aged 59 or older at the spouse's death. Either way, you must own the home and occupy it as your main residence on January 1. The auditor shows a $40,000 income ceiling for 2024 applicants, indexed each September, and describes the credit as the tax on $28,000 of true value. Call the auditor for the figures that apply this year. Use form DTE 105A to apply and DTE 105E for a disability certificate. A prior-year application filed late is accepted through December 31.

For farmland, DTE 109 requests current agricultural use value. ORC 5713.30 requires at least ten acres in commercial agricultural use during the three years before filing, or fewer than ten acres that averaged $2,500 or more in gross yearly income. If a sale ends that status, a recoupment charge covering the tax savings can follow.

Do repairs or additions before a sale need permits?

They can. The county building regulation office at 520 S. Broadway, 937-547-7379, wants permits and inspections for electrical, heating and cooling, and construction work, residential or commercial, with construction meaning all new building, additions and replacements. Its territory is the unincorporated area, Greenville, and the villages of Ansonia, Arcanum, Castine, Gettysburg, Ithaca, New Madison, New Weston, Pitsburg, Union City, Versailles, Wayne Lakes and Yorkshire.

A building permit application needs drawings showing a foundation plan, a floor plan, bearing wall cross sections, roof detail and exterior elevations. Construction also needs sign-off from the Darke County Health Department at 937-548-4196. Zoning is separate: cities, villages and townships hold that authority, and owners in an unzoned area contact a township trustee. The zoning inspector at 937-547-7381 answers questions about a township's zoning and about splitting off a lot.

Ask the building office which permits your repairs need before you list, and keep the approved paperwork in your sale file.

Property tax when a Darke County house sells

Before the deed reaches the recorder, the buyer files a conveyance fee statement with the auditor using form DTE 100 (DTE 100EX if an exemption applies). At that moment the seller owes the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax, and the auditor stamps the deed.

The statement asks about homestead and farmland. If the property carried a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction, both sides sign a sworn instrument covering how that reduction ends. Farmland that was under agricultural valuation gets its own statement on form DTE 102. The auditor's conveyance fee calculator adds the parcel transfer fee to the total, so you can estimate costs before closing.

When tax is delinquent, the treasurer's payoff figure lets the title company build it into the closing numbers. A buyer paying cash faces the same steps, and clearing them early keeps a quick closing on track.

Which office issues a Darke County tax bill?

The treasurer, at 937-547-7365. The auditor's real estate division, at 937-547-7308, answers questions about the value behind the bill.

The deadline is March 31 of the following tax year, or the end of first-half collection if later. File the DTE 1 with the auditor.

Does Darke County have a tax credit for older owners?

Yes. The Ohio homestead program covers owners aged 65 or older, disabled owners and qualifying surviving spouses. Apply on DTE 105A and ask the auditor which income limit applies.

Yes. Get a payoff figure from the treasurer, and use the auditor's delinquency report to see what is posted against the parcel.

The city of Delaware is the seat, and Powell, Sunbury and parts of Dublin and Westerville lie inside the county, as do the villages Ashley, Galena, Ostrander and Shawnee Hills. The bill changes with the school district, so look at the district on your parcel record. A buyer comparing monthly costs will do the same, because identical house values can produce different bills from one district to the next.

Property tax due dates

Payment comes in two installments. For tax year 2026 bills, the first installment is due February 10, 2027 and the second July 12, 2027. Billing runs a year behind, so bills for one tax year are collected the next.

  • Forms on the treasurer's site cover for the 2 1/2% reduction, escrow or ACH automatic deduction, homestead, penalty remission, property valuation complaint and a tax mailing address change.
  • Past payments appear on the auditor's parcel record: open the Tax tab and scroll to the bottom of the Tax Detail screen.
  • A one-time change moved the 2025 second-half deadline in 2026, and collections return to the usual February and July pattern.

For a question about one bill, phone the treasurer at (740) 833-2480.

What House Bill 186 changed on Delaware County bills

Under House Bill 186, an Inflation Cap Credit trims taxes on certain school district levies, and it reached back to tax year 2025 for real property. Residential and agricultural parcels receive it everywhere in the county except in the Dublin, Westerville and Olentangy school districts.

Owners who qualified and had already paid in full see any overpayment applied to the following tax year. The credit shows as its own line on the second-half bill and on the property record at the auditor's site. The treasurer also posted a summary of the bill on its home page. A seller preparing a listing should pull the parcel's tax detail from the auditor's site rather than quote an old bill to a buyer.

How to contest your value with the Board of Revision

Send a formal complaint to the auditor during the window that opens January 2 and closes March 31. The board looks at what the property was worth on the January 1 lien date, and it hears value only, not complaints about the tax rate or the taxes. The deadline set in Ohio Revised Code 5715.19 is March 31, unless first-half collection runs past it.

For the 2026 triennial valuation update, a formal complaint against the value as of January 1, 2027 must be in by March 31, 2027. Complaints can be handed in at the auditor's office, mailed to 145 N. Union St., emailed to auditor@co.delaware.oh.us, or faxed to (740) 833-2899.

  • Helpful attachments: a recent independent appraisal, photos of damage, comparable sales, plus the purchase contract and closing statement for a house that just sold.
  • Hearings run like a short court session, with sworn witnesses and marked exhibits, and usually take 10 to 20 minutes.
  • Decisions sit for 30 days before values change. Still unhappy? The next stops are the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas, and the 30 days run from the date on the decision letter.
  • The board will not cut a value just because the auditor's figures for neighbors look lower, when those neighbors had no arm's length sale.

Homestead exemption and disclosure at closing

The homestead exemption is the big one, and it follows the owner instead of the house. For owners 65 and older, or anyone permanently and totally disabled, it removes the tax on $25,000 of market value, covering a home plus up to one acre. First-time applicants must pass an income test. A person who got the credit for tax year 2013 is exempt from that test and carries the credit to a new Ohio home.

State law adds a disclosure step at the deed stage. ORC 319.202 requires the buyer's value statement to say that the seller was asked whether the property receives a tax reduction under section 323.152(A) and whether it was in current agricultural use valuation. If it was, the paperwork has to account for the lost reduction or the recoupment charge before the auditor endorses the deed.

Selling with unpaid Delaware County tax

Find out the exact balance with the treasurer before you set an asking price, and have the closing agent request a payoff so the tax is cleared at the sale. The treasurer's website carries a Tax Lien Sales page with a tax lien certificate sale policy, and the auditor's site has a Forfeited Land Sales page, so a long delinquency can end in a county process.

The treasurer's forms page lists a Penalty Remission form. Call (740) 833-2480 to ask whether it applies to a given parcel. Owners who are behind and short on time can also line up a buyer first and let the closing statement show the tax balance as a line item.

Here is a short checklist. Pull the parcel's tax detail from the auditor's site, call the treasurer for the balance, ask the closing agent to order the payoff, and keep the paid receipts. A cash sale still settles the tax from proceeds, so the same steps apply. Cash buyers often ask for the payoff in writing, and having it ready lets you accept an offer without delay.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Delaware County auditor's office?

The office is on the 1st floor at 145 N. Union St., Delaware, OH 43015, phone (740) 833-2900. Weekday hours are 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Who do I call about a Delaware County tax bill?

Call the Delaware County Treasurer at (740) 833-2480. The treasurer shares the 145 N. Union St. building with the auditor and takes questions on payments, escrow and penalties.

Who can file a Delaware County value complaint?

Any owner of taxable real property in the county, the owner's spouse, and a retained professional such as an appraiser, broker or public accountant can file under ORC 5715.19. The Board of Revision handles value only, not the rate.

Did every Delaware County owner get the Inflation Cap Credit?

No. Residential and agricultural parcels received it except those in the Dublin, Westerville and Olentangy school districts, and not every property qualifies.

What is the Delaware County property tax rate?

It depends on the parcel's school district, township or city, and voted levies. The auditor posts a Rates of Taxation page and an Effective Tax Rates page, and the parcel's own record shows its figures.

Billing lags a year. A levy approved by voters counts for its own tax year, yet you pay it the year after. Who handles property tax in Franklin County

Franklin County divides tax duties among three offices. Appraisals and ownership records sit with the Auditor. Billing and collection belong to the Treasurer. Arguments over value go to the Board of Revision. Choosing the right one first saves a few transferred calls.

  • Auditor: 373 S. High Street, 21st floor, Columbus; phone 614-525-4663. Values, homestead applications, transfers and the farmland valuation program (CAUV).

  • Board of Revision: phone 614-525-3913, email BOR@franklincountyohio.gov. Complaints about appraised value.

Behind the scenes, the Auditor's real estate division covers 483,319 parcels and handles more than $2 billion in tax collections for more than 85 entities countywide.

Due dates and payment options

Choose how to pay: all at once early in the year, in two halves, or monthly. Half one lands in late February or early March and half two lands in July, which was July 20 for the 2026 collection.

Bills reflect the prior year, and payment is possible only once the Auditor has assessed the property. The Budget Payment Program lets you prepay monthly into an escrow account in your name, which is applied automatically when the semi-annual bill comes due. Under Ohio Revised Code 7.16, the county posts its full tax rate listing on the Columbus Dispatch website.

To pay by mail, send the billing statement and a check payable to the Franklin County Treasurer, with your parcel number and a daytime phone number on the check. Add a stamped envelope addressed to yourself for a receipt. A kiosk at the office takes credit cards through the secure payment site. If a payment bounces, the Treasurer reverses it after the bank reports back, usually in two to three business days. No returned item fee is charged, yet a missed due date can still bring a penalty.

How the county values your house

Under Ohio law every parcel is reappraised on a six-year cycle, with an update at the halfway point. Franklin County's full reappraisal was done in 2023, and the update followed in 2026.

Between cycles, a parcel's value moves for just three reasons:

  • physical changes such as a new porch, patio or deck
  • demolition of a structure
  • a Board of Revision decision on a filed complaint

Rate times value gives the bill, so any cut in value reduces what you owe. The Distribution tab on the Treasurer's property search shows where your money goes: the school district, municipality, library and other entities.

How to contest your value

A value complaint begins at the Board of Revision. For tax year 2026, the Auditor's office takes valuation complaints from November 20, 2026 until March 31, 2027.

The Board checks the Auditor's appraised value and can revise it when the evidence supports a change. Good evidence includes a closing statement, a purchase contract or an appraisal. Zoom is the default hearing format, with in-person available if you ask at least 10 days in advance. Mediation, a less formal route, is used in some cases. Only value is in play here. The rate and the dollars owed are beyond the Board's authority.

An unhappy owner gets 30 days from the mailing date of the ruling to appeal, either to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or to the Court of Common Pleas. Copy the notice to the Board of Revision, and to the County Auditor when filing in court.

Tax relief programs

Apply separately for each program:

The total income cap is $41,000 for applications tied to a 2025 return. Mail to Franklin County Auditor, Homestead, 373 S High St, 21st Floor, or email homestead@franklincountyohio.gov.
  • Enhanced homestead exemption: covers service members who are 100% disabled from service-connected injuries, plus surviving spouses of public service officers killed in the line of duty. There is no income test, and approval shields $50,000 of appraised value from tax.
  • Current Agricultural Use Valuation (CAUV): farmland valued by soil type. File or renew by the first Monday of March.
  • Penalty remission: form 23-A, filed with the Treasurer's Office, asks that a late-payment penalty be forgiven.
  • Delinquent tax payment plans: the Treasurer offers plans to bring a past due account current.

Around 40,000 Franklin County parcels receive some tax incentive such as an abatement or a tax increment financing arrangement.

What a sale does to your taxes

Any change of ownership stops at the Auditor before the Recorder. Expect a conveyance fee of $3 per $1,000 of price, falling to $1 per $1,000 when the seller currently receives the homestead exemption, plus a $0.50 transfer charge on each non-exempt transfer.

R.C. 319.202 has the buyer's statement of value report whether the seller claimed a homestead or owner-occupancy reduction and whether the land was under farm use valuation. If a reduction exists, the two sides settle the estimated amount between themselves. Land leaving the farm program can trigger a recoupment charge.

Because bills come in arrears, the closing statement is where the year gets divided. Have the title agent pull current payment status from the Treasurer's property search. Raise any penalty remission with the Treasurer before closing. Sellers who are behind can ask about a delinquent payment plan.

Owing back taxes does not stop a sale, since they are paid out of the proceeds. Find the balance on the Treasurer's property search, then call 614-525-3438 for the payoff figure the title agent will ask for anyway. To seek a reduced penalty, send in form 23-A ahead of closing.

With a cash buyer there is no lender to wait on, so closing can be quick, which helps when a bill is already late. The Auditor's transfer still comes first. Arrange the deed, the notary and both payments before heading downtown.

About Franklin County

Columbus, the county seat, anchors the Columbus metropolitan area. Franklin County led Ohio in 2020 with 1,323,807 people in 540,369 households. Neighbors are Delaware, Fairfield, Licking, Madison, Pickaway and Union counties.

Homes in Dublin, Gahanna, Hilliard and Westerville are all billed by the county Treasurer, though each parcel's rate follows the school district and municipality that cover it.

July, and it was July 20 for the 2026 collection. Late payments pick up penalty and interest whether or not a bill reached you.

Where do I file a Franklin County property value complaint?

File it with the Board of Revision by way of the Auditor's office. The window for tax year 2026 runs November 20, 2026 through March 31, 2027.

Which Franklin County office answers questions about a tax bill?

The Treasurer, at 614-525-3438. For value questions use the Auditor at 614-525-4663, and for complaints use the Board of Revision at 614-525-3913.

Can I pay Franklin County property taxes monthly?

Yes. Monthly installments are allowed, and the Budget Payment Program holds your prepayments in an escrow account in your name until the bill comes due.

Is the Franklin County conveyance fee lower for homestead sellers?

Yes. It drops from $3 to $1 per $1,000 of price if the seller has the homestead exemption when the transfer happens.

Its field appraisers visit every property that was issued a building or zoning permit during the year.

Homestead exemption and other relief

The Homestead Exemption shields $29,000 of a home's market value from local taxes, and the average Geauga savings is about $518 a year. In the Auditor's example, a $100,000 home would be billed as if it were worth $71,000.

  • Seniors: turn 65 by the end of 2026 and keep household income below $41,000, measured as 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income.

Damaged or destroyed property

The Auditor can lower the value of real estate hurt by fire, flood, ice or other causes, but cannot issue refunds for earlier years. File the damaged property application as soon as possible. The deduction depends on the calendar quarter of the damage.

Damage from January through March earns a 100 percent deduction and April through June earns 75 percent, and the deadline for both is December 31. July through September earns 50 percent with the same deadline. October through December earns 25 percent, with a January 31 deadline. The reduction stays until the property is restored.

Taxes at a Geauga County closing

Deeds go to the Auditor for transfer before they are recorded. The Auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of transfer value plus $0.50 per parcel, and the tax records are updated as the parcel changes hands.

Get the balance on the parcel from the Treasurer, then confirm with your title company who pays the February and July installments. If taxes on a parcel were missed, the Auditor's Forfeited Land Sale page is the place to look. A cash sale needs the same payoff figure, so request it before you set a closing date.

Geauga County in brief

The 2020 count was 95,397 people. Owners occupy 87.2 percent of the housing stock, the median home they own is worth $331,100, and the median household earns $107,860. The county issued 180 building permits in 2025. Chardon, Burton, Middlefield and South Russell are among its municipalities, and a November 2024 vote dissolved the Village of Aquilla.

When are Geauga County property taxes due?

The second Wednesday in February covers the first half and the second Wednesday in July covers the second half. The Treasurer mails the bills ahead of each date, in January and June.

How much can the Geauga County homestead exemption save?

The exemption shields $29,000 of market value, with average savings of about $518 a year. You must apply on paper with the Auditor by December 31 and meet the age or disability and income rules.

Where does a Geauga County value dispute start?

Ask the Auditor's appraisal office for an informal review first. If that fails, a complaint to the Board of Revision must reach the Auditor by the end of the following March, or when first-half collection closes if that is later.

Will the Geauga County Treasurer text me a tax bill?

No. The Treasurer sends bills only by regular mail. A text message asking for a tax payment is fraudulent and should be deleted.

Which number reaches the Geauga County real estate tax staff?

Questions about values, exemptions and credits go to the Auditor's real estate line, (440) 279-1617. The main Auditor number is (440) 279-1600, answered on weekdays between 8:00 and 4:30.

How often Hamilton County revalues homes

State law has each county auditor re-value every property twice per six-year cycle. The auditor's valuation page places Hamilton County's full reappraisal in 2023, a desktop triennial update in 2026 and the next reappraisal in 2030, across upward of 350,000 parcels.

The 2026 update is a statistical sweep of recent sales, so nobody walks through your house. Staff keep inspecting permitted projects and new construction every year. These values drive tax year 2026, payable 2027. The property search tool refreshes once the state confirms the numbers, typically toward year end, and Value Change Notice letters arrive by mail.

A jump in value does not lift your taxes by the same percentage. Levies, credits and exemptions set the bill, and reduction factors on voted levies aim to hold their revenue near last year's level. New construction and newly approved levies are what bring in more.

Cincinnati holds the courthouse and the biggest population, and the 2020 census made Hamilton the third-largest county in Ohio. A 2025 estimate of 838,418 residents sits 0.9 percent above the 2020 base.

House Bill 186 limits inflation-driven growth from unvoted levies that would flow to schools sitting at the 20-mill floor, with a 2-mill floor for career-technical districts. Evidence goes in with the complaint or up to ten days ahead of the hearing. A hearing lasts around 15 minutes, and a certified-mail result follows in six to eight weeks. To challenge that result, file with the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the Court of Common Pleas within 30 days of the mailing.

Tax foreclosure is a lawsuit the county prosecutor files for the treasurer, with a typical 28 days for the owner to answer and sheriff sales held online.

Selling with taxes owed

Each parcel gets its own bill, so a home on several parcels needs every bill totaled before the payoff. The stadium tax credit is automatic when a property already receives the 2.5 percent rollback.

Numbers worth keeping handy: the Auditor's real estate staff at (440) 350-2532 for owner address changes and credit questions, the Treasurer's billing line at (440) 350-2516 and the delinquent tax division at 440-350-2473. Pay after the deadline and a 10 percent penalty is added, with interest running twice a year on balances the county certifies as unpaid. A postal postmark on or before the date counts. Section 323.13 contains a rule many owners miss: the tax is owed whether or not a bill reached you. Call if nothing shows up by February 1 or July 1. Bills go out in mid-January and mid-June, with payment due roughly 20 to 30 days afterward. Manufactured homes run on their own calendar, also posted by the Treasurer.

How to challenge your property value

A Lake County owner can contest the valuation but never the rate. The filing season for a complaint on form DTE 1 runs January 1 to March 31 every year, and the next one opens January 1, 2027.

  • A three person panel hears the case: the Auditor, the Treasurer and the commissioners' president.
  • Bring proof with the complaint, or file it at least five days before your hearing date.
  • Expect roughly a quarter hour for a house, then a written decision about two to three weeks later.
  • Evidence the county names: a recent arm's length sale, a purchase agreement or listing, an appraisal dated to the January 1 lien date, damage photos, an insurance value, a broker's market analysis, or construction cost for a newer home including land.
  • Arguments the Board cannot weigh: how much your bill went up in percent, and how nearby parcels were valued.

The first affects the July 2026 bill, where applicable credits or reductions are printed. Residential, agricultural and most business properties qualify without an application, and the Treasurer advises contacting your mortgage company once the credit shows so the escrow payment can be adjusted.

The homestead credit is doubled for 2026 tax payable in 2027, while the owner occupancy credit is not. For the details, call the Auditor's real estate desk at 440-350-2532. The homestead exemption is means tested for new participants, so ask for the current household income limit before you apply.

An ordinary sale settles the current year's tax at closing, usually through a title company. The county's pro-rating page is written for sheriff sales: after a sale is confirmed, the Treasurer gives the total due at that time and prorates the following year's tax from the current year's full-year real estate tax plus long-term assessments such as lighting or storm water. The deed transfer charge is a separate line at the Auditor: $4.00 per $1,000 of price plus fifty cents for each parcel. Section 319.202 assigns it to the seller. An administrative fee of $100.00 applies with the first notice and $200.00 on the sale date, and the sale is generally held every fall.
  • Lien sales can lead to 18 percent interest and added fees.
  • The Treasurer holds the first and best lien on real property. A lien purchaser can ask for foreclosure if the lien is not repaid or on a plan within 18 months, and the county prosecutor can also file in the Treasurer's name, which may lead to a sheriff sale.

Five townships, nine villages, nine cities, ten school districts and eight library systems share each bill, so a parcel's total rate depends on which of those districts it sits in. Ask the Auditor which districts your parcel falls into before you quote taxes to a buyer.

Only the value is open to challenge. The rate comes from levies, and the Board does not hear complaints about taxes. Use form DTE 1 during the January 1 to March 31 season.

The Auditor charges $4.00 per $1,000 of price and $0.50 per parcel. That splits into a state piece of $1.00 and a county piece of $3.00, the latter passed by the commissioners on March 26, 1990.

What is the penalty on late Lake County property tax?

Ten percent, with twice-a-year interest on certified balances. A missing bill is no excuse under section 323.13. A payment plan can keep the debt from growing.

New Albany alone adds more than 100 homes a year beside a nine-million-square-foot business park, which keeps pressure on land values at the county's western edge.

Who runs value and collection

The county splits the job between two desks at 20 South Second Street in Newark. A delinquent balance gets settled with the treasurer, whose office collects overdue real estate tax and assessments.

Special assessments sit with the treasurer as well. Ask which ones are open on the parcel so the closing figures include them.

Selling with taxes owed

Owing tax does not stop a sale, but it changes the order of events. Ask the treasurer for the amount due, including any ten percent charge, interest and open special assessments. Give that figure to your title company so it can be paid from the proceeds at closing. Ask the auditor, since the tax exists only where commissioners passed a resolution for it. The state conveyance fee is a separate charge that the seller pays at the auditor's counter.

Both offices work out of the Lorain County Administration Building, 226 Middle Avenue, Elyria. The auditor occupies Room 200 and answers at 440-329-5207. Lorain County was reappraised in 2024. House Bill 186 adds an Inflation Cap Credit that applies automatically when school-related taxes rise faster than inflation after a reappraisal. Anyone who paid before the credit posted needs to do nothing, because the overpayment carries into the next first-half bill. The law did not change appraised values.

Due dates and penalties

A late half costs ten percent under Ohio Revised Code 323.121, reduced by half if the money arrives within ten days. Title and mortgage companies that generate and print their own bills skip the duplicate bill fee.

How to dispute your value

A Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property goes in after January 1 and by March 31. The rules:

  • Signature and notary seal are required, and owner, address and parcel numbers must be right.
  • Ordinary mail works, and the postmark counts as the filing date.

Local school boards may also petition the board. The hearing schedule and a case search are on the auditor's site.

Tax reductions that matter at a sale

Conveyances reach the auditor in person or by e-file. Mailed transfers are not accepted. Staff cannot fill in conveyance forms or advise on them under Ohio Revised Code 4705.01, so paperwork falls to a title company or lawyer.

Rental property adds a duty under Ohio Revised Code 5323.02: the owner names a contact agent to the auditor within 60 days of the conveyance filing, or risks a penalty of up to $150 on the parcel. A conveyance fee calculator on the auditor's site takes the sale amount and the number of parcels.

Call 440-329-5787 and ask the treasurer for the current balance on the parcel before you set a closing date. Home improvements that raise an assessment

The auditor's appraisal page separates upkeep from additions. Repairs that are not part of a complete modernization can be made without raising the tax. Exterior items include painting, landscaping, new gutters, siding repair, storm windows, fencing and a replaced driveway. Interior items include rewiring, new plumbing, drywall repair, a replacement water heater and a furnace swapped for the same type.

These changes may add to the taxable value:

  • Fireplaces, new porches or decks, and room additions.
  • Added bathrooms, stall showers or other new plumbing fixtures.
  • Finishing an attic or basement.
  • A new or larger garage, and central air conditioning.
  • In-ground pools, and farm outbuildings, silos and grain bins.

An owner who tore down a dilapidated shed, garage or barn files a Razing Affidavit, DTE 26, so the building comes off the tax list. File it before a sale so a building that no longer stands does not show on the bill.

Payment deadlines

Lucas County bills come in two installments, and the dates are printed right on the bill. Treasurer staff post the coming date once the bills go out. Under section 323.17, a delayed tax duplicate can push the payment dates to January 31 and July 20, so the dates are not identical every year.

Paying by mail is where people get caught. A USPS postmark can carry a date a day or more after you drop the envelope, and Ohio law treats the postmark as the payment date. The Treasurer offers three workarounds:

  • Send the check well before the due date.
  • Ask for a hand-stamped postmark at the post office counter.
  • Pay online, which is available at any time.

A payment plan option is also available. Ask the Treasurer's office for the terms before you fall behind.

How to contest your value

The Board of Revision takes complaints starting January 1 and ending at the close of March. The board has three seats: Auditor, Treasurer and one Commissioner, or their delegates. It hears disputes about value and nothing else, so levy and rate complaints go elsewhere.

Lucas County Board of Revision steps
StepWhat to do
Filing windowJanuary 1 to March 31
FormDTE Form 1, 1M or 2, filed on paper (notarized) or online
Hearing30-minute slot, in person, by phone or by video
EvidenceSubmit at least 5 days before the hearing

The burden is on you. Bring nearby comparable sales, your own recent purchase price or a private appraisal. For a house damaged or torn down, a separate DTE 26 application adjusts value starting the next tax year.

What happens to your tax while a complaint is pending

You may pay based on your own figure. Section 5715.19 requires the Treasurer to accept a payment computed on the value stated in your complaint while the complaint is pending. If the final value turns out higher than what you paid, interest runs on the shortfall from the original due date, so keep the complaint number handy when you pay.

Four more points from the statute:

  • The filing window stays open to the later of March 31 or the close of first-half collection.
  • After the last filing day the board has 180 days to decide.
  • Filing again on the same parcel in the same interim period takes a changed fact, such as an arm's length sale, storm or fire loss, or a major improvement.
  • Papers you hold back from the board may be barred if you appeal later.

If you plan to sell this year, a pending complaint can still matter to the buyer. Give the title company the complaint number and the value you stated, since the tax that was paid at that figure may be adjusted once the board rules.

Homestead exemption and other relief

Lucas County offers homestead relief in four forms. An owner who is 65 or older, or totally and permanently disabled, can claim it on the house they live in when 2025 taxable income was $41,000 or less. A spouse's taxable income counts toward that cap, though Social Security does not. Owners rated or compensated at 100 percent for a service-connected disability qualify without an income limit. Surviving spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty can qualify for an enhanced version.

For tax year 2025, payable in 2026, the exempted value is $29,000, and that amount doubles for the service-connected disability and surviving spouse tracks. It reduces taxable value on your primary residence and nothing else. Questions go to Homestead@co.lucas.oh.us or 419-213-4406.

When the home sells, Ohio's value statement asks the buyer to confirm with the seller whether the property carries these reductions or the agricultural use valuation, as section 319.202 requires. Answer it accurately, since a reduction may end with the sale.

Selling with taxes owed

Deeds pass through the Auditor before recording. The Auditor's transfer fact sheet lists $0.50 per parcel plus $4.00 for each $1,000 of price. Death, survivorship and own-trust transfers are generally exempt from the larger charge.

Unpaid tax stays attached to the parcel, so get the Treasurer's balance for yours before signing a contract. At closing the title company pays what is owed from your proceeds. A cash buyer can move fast, but the balance still has to be cleared before the deed is recorded. Ask the Treasurer or your title agent for a payoff figure a few days before closing, and bring your latest bill and parcel number to the table. If a Board of Revision complaint is pending, tell the title company so the payment is figured on the right number.

Frequently asked questions

By what date must I contest a Lucas County value?

March 31. The Board of Revision accepts complaints from January 1 through March 31. State law allows the later date of March 31 or the close of first-half collection for the tax year.

Can the Lucas County Board of Revision lower my tax rate?

No. The board hears appeals on property values only, not on the taxes themselves. Levy rates come from votes in your taxing district.

How do I prove a Lucas County value is wrong?

Bring evidence such as comparable neighborhood sales, a recent sale of the property or a private appraisal. The burden of proof sits with the owner who files.

Who qualifies for the Lucas County homestead exemption?

Homeowners aged 65 or more, or totally and permanently disabled, who live in the house and had $41,000 or less in 2025 taxable income. Owners rated 100 percent disabled through military service and surviving spouses of first responders killed on duty also qualify, with a larger exempted amount.

Is a postmarked check still safe for a Lucas County tax payment?

Not always. USPS postmarks can show a later date than the day you mail, and Ohio law uses the postmark date. Pay online or request a hand-stamped postmark.
