Which offices handle a Mahoning County tax bill

A bill passes through three hands. The auditor sets each parcel's value and builds the tax list, the treasurer takes in payments, and the Board of Revision rules on disputes over value. Call the auditor at 330-740-2010 for forms and exemptions. The treasurer's counter is on the courthouse ground level at 120 Market Street, Youngstown, with phones at 330-740-2460 and weekday hours that end at 4:30 in the afternoon.

The auditor has no say over rates. Each school board, township, city and the county submits a budget, voters approve the levies, and the state tax department's procedures turn them into rates. An owner unhappy with a rate should attend budget hearings and write to those taxing bodies.

Mahoning County housing market

Mahoning County sits on Ohio's eastern edge, next to Pennsylvania, with Youngstown as the seat and largest city. Population was 224,706 in the 2025 estimate, down from 228,614 in 2020. The market is modestly priced:

  • Typical value of a home that its owner lives in: $154,700
  • Share of homes occupied by owners: 70.3 percent
  • Gross rent at the midpoint: $791 a month
  • Households: 98,065, at 2.25 people each

Twenty public school districts divide the county, among them Youngstown City, Boardman, Canfield, Poland, Austintown, Struthers and Western Reserve. School levies drive much of a bill, so the district listed on the parcel record shapes what an owner pays.

How value is set and what caps an increase

Under Ohio law the taxable amount is 35 percent of market value. Every parcel is revalued on a six-year cycle, with appraisers checking exteriors each time. Market value means the price a willing seller would take from a willing buyer. Appraisers study sales and apply them to the property record, so a wrong bedroom count or a missing garage can raise a value without the owner noticing.

Two limits soften increases. A 1976 law, House Bill 920, grants a credit against voted millage so that a reappraisal does not raise what existing levies collect. A newer measure, House Bill 186, set up an inflation cap credit for certain property classes. Applying it meant a one-time mid-cycle rate change from the state, and any overpayment will be returned as a credit or refund.

Timing surprises sellers too. Taxes are collected a year behind and a parcel is judged as it stood on January 1. A demolished garage may keep appearing on a bill, and a split or merger recorded this year reaches the tax list the year after.

Due dates and ways to pay

A postmark often reflects the day a postal machine first handled the envelope, possibly days after you dropped it off. Paying electronically, mailing early, or requesting a hand-stamped mark at the retail counter avoids that risk.

How to appeal your assessment

The route is a written complaint against the valuation, sent to the Board of Revision. Three officeholders sit on it by statute: the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president, with two forming a quorum. Complaints are accepted from January until the end of March each year.

A hearing deals with value only. Rates and the size of the bill are outside its reach, and the person complaining has to make the case. Bring:

  • A sale within the last 24 months, with the settlement statement and a notarized arm's-length affidavit
  • A tax-purpose appraisal from a certified appraiser
  • Photographs paired with professional repair estimates

Feuds with neighbors, nearby pets, sewer trouble, and the fact that you never improved the property carry no weight. Send the form to the Board at the auditor's office or hand-deliver it. The Board takes no responsibility for lost mail, so keep following up until a date-stamped copy reaches you.

Homestead and other tax relief

Residential and farm parcels get a non-business credit with no paperwork. The owner-occupancy credit needs an application unless the owner already receives it. The auditor also describes:

  • Homestead Exemption. Open to resident owners who are 65 or older, permanently disabled, or a qualifying surviving spouse, within an income limit. The value shielded in 2025 was $29,000, doubling to $58,000 in the enhanced version for owners with a service-connected disability and surviving spouses of public service officers, which has no income test.
  • CAUV farm valuation. Tracts of ten acres or more used solely for commercial farming qualify, as does smaller land averaging $2,500 a year in sales. The auditor must receive the application between the first Monday of January and the first Monday of March; a postmark alone does not count.
  • Recoupment. Dropping out of CAUV triggers a charge equal to three years of taxes, a point any farm seller should raise with the auditor before closing.

The state updates CAUV soil values every three years, with the next change applying to tax year 2026.

Selling with taxes owed

Begin with the balance owed. Delinquent taxes are handled by the treasurer at 330-740-2460, so get a figure before a buyer signs. Charges levied by outside bodies, for example lighting or grass cutting, are folded into the tax breakdown. Mortgages, mechanic's claims and judgments never show on the bill. The recorder at 330-740-2345 and the Clerk of Courts at 330-740-2104 can speak to those.

Then prepare the deed. Land described in acres or part of a platted lot must first be reviewed at the GIS and Tax Map table, 21 West Boardman Street. The auditor's checklist also asks for the seller's marital status, the buyer's tax mailing address, a legal description and the prior deed reference. A sale costs $1.00 per $1,000 of price for the conveyance fee, $3.00 per $1,000 for the permissive fee and 50 cents a parcel to transfer, so have the auditor confirm the total.

Whatever shape the house is in, unpaid taxes will turn up in the title search, and the treasurer can settle them ahead of closing. A cash buyer skips the lender's payoff, but not the tax balance.

Frequently asked questions

Which office answers questions about a Mahoning County bill?

The treasurer, at 330-740-2460, handles payments and balances. The auditor, at 330-740-2010, handles value, exemptions and forms. Both work from 120 Market Street in Youngstown.

When does the complaint window close each year?

On March 31. The Board of Revision accepts value complaints from January through the end of March.

Can repair needs lower my valuation?

They can, when documented. Photographs plus a contractor's estimate are accepted, though the owner must show the value is too high. A general objection to higher taxes will fail.

Does the treasurer take credit cards?

Yes, online or by phone. Expect a 2.5 percent card fee with a $2.00 floor and $1.50 per e-check payment, and these go to the payment vendor.

Does selling CAUV farmland trigger a penalty?

It may. Withdrawing or no longer qualifying brings a charge of three years of taxes. Acreage can stay enrolled if the new owner applies or the former owner renewed on time, so check with the auditor first.

Who collects property tax in Medina County

The Medina County Treasurer collects the bill. The office is in the County Administration Building at 144 North Broadway in Medina, and the phone number is 330-725-9748. The counter is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays, and stays open until 6:00 p.m. on a due date.

Two offices split the work. The auditor values the parcels and handles exemptions. The treasurer sends the bills and takes the payments. The treasurer's website, which is separate from the auditor's, is where you look up a bill and pay it.

Bills come out twice a year. If yours never shows up, call the office or use the Search and Pay Taxes link on the treasurer's site. It lets you print an official bill to pay by mail or at the counter, so a missing bill is never a reason to miss the date.

Housing in Medina County

Medina County sits in northeast Ohio, south and west of Cleveland. The 2020 census counted 182,470 residents, up from 172,332 in 2010, and the 2025 estimate is 185,025. Growth like that keeps demand for homes steady.

Due dates and penalties

Ohio bills property tax in two halves. The 2026 first half came due February 27 and the second half August 28. Both dates ran later than in earlier years, when deadlines fell in early or mid February and in July. The second-half bills were late because the county auditor had to reprogram software for a new state law, and every one of Ohio's 88 counties had delays. The treasurer announces future dates each time bills go out, so look for the current notice instead of assuming last year's calendar.

How to pay a Medina County tax bill

  • Phone. Call 1-888-607-8389 to pay by e-check or card, with the same fees.

What is the inflation cap credit?

House Bill 186 created a credit that limits increases on certain unvoted school taxes to the rate of inflation. Six of Medina County's eight school districts fell under the state's 20 mill floor: Black River, Brunswick, Buckeye, Cloverleaf, Highland and the Career Center. After the auditor's 2025 reappraisal raised values, those districts received more than $14 million in additional unvoted revenue. The cap sends about $5.5 million back to taxpayers, and it appears on the second-half bill as Inflation Cap Credit.

Not every owner gets it, because only six of the eight districts were affected. If a second-half bill shows no credit and you think it should, ask the auditor's office about the parcel before you assume the bill is wrong.

Homestead reduction for seniors and disabled owners

In December 2025 the Ohio legislature doubled the tax reduction for qualified homestead owners. It first showed on first-half 2026 bills as a separate line called Local Homestead Reduction. About 11,500 of the county's 67,700 homeowners are estimated to qualify. The amount depends on local millage, and in two districts the treasurer checked it came to $354 in one township and $504 in another.

To qualify you must own and live in the home and meet one of these conditions:

  • Age 65 or older
  • Permanent and total disability
  • A veteran, or the spouse of a first responder killed in the line of duty

Call the auditor's office at 330-725-9754 for the current form before you file. The board rules on the appraised value of the property. Local taxing bodies put the levies on the ballot, and a complaint cannot change them. If you win a lower value, the bill drops with it, but the rate stays the same.

Selling with taxes owed

Request a current balance from the treasurer at 330-725-9748 and look up the parcel through Search and Pay Taxes. Ohio bills a year in arrears, so a sale in the first half of a year can leave the second-half installment for the prior tax year unpaid. Bring the latest bill, the parcel number and your closing contact to any call. Staff can then read you the exact balance, including any penalty that has been added, and tell you whether a payment is still pending.

330-725-9748 reaches the County Treasurer. For homestead applications, call the County Auditor at 330-725-9754.

February 27, 2026 for the first half and August 28, 2026 for the second half. A mailed payment had to be postmarked on or before those dates to avoid the 5 percent penalty.

It is 5 percent for payments after the due date and 10 percent once a later date passes. In 2026 that later date was March 9 for the first half and September 7 for the second half.

Twenty-four hour drop boxes are at the Treasurer's office in Medina, Brunswick City Hall, the Lodi Library and the Wadsworth Municipal Building. Include the bill stub.

Miami County, Ohio: parcels and school districts

Miami County belongs to the Dayton metropolitan area, with Shelby County to the north, Champaign and Clark to the east, Montgomery to the south and Darke to the west. The auditor counts 54,707 parcels. Troy holds the courthouse and is the largest city, Piqua and Tipp City are cities too, and Huber Heights and Union each extend partly into the county.

Troy, Piqua, Tipp City, Covington, Milton-Union, Miami East, Newton, Bradford and Bethel each have their own public school district. The district that serves a house decides several of the levies printed on its bill, so name it in any listing conversation about taxes.

Who owns homes here

As of July 2025 the county counted 112,634 residents, up 3.5 percent from 2020. Nearly three in four households (73.4 percent) own, among 44,906 households in all.

  • The middle owner-occupied house is valued at $229,100.
  • Monthly owner costs run $1,453 with a mortgage and $549 without one.
  • Gross rent is $966 at the median.

About a quarter of occupied homes are rentals, so a sale with a tenant in place is nothing unusual in Troy or Piqua.

How the auditor sets a value

Every sixth year Ohio requires a complete reappraisal, with an update midway between, and taxable value is 35 percent of market value. Each parcel has a record at the auditor's that the public may inspect. Ask which year the next update lands.

The auditor cannot change a tax rate. Rates reflect budget requests by local governments and votes by residents, and a bill equals the rate times the valuation on the general tax list. Absent a vote, Ohio limits taxation to ten mills. Every levy beyond that was approved at the polls. Special assessments for ditches, paving, curbs, sidewalks, sewers or water lines show up as their own line on the bill.

Before you list, pull your parcel record from the auditor's office and read it. A wrong square footage, room count or condition entry can inflate the value, and fixing it is easier before a buyer asks about the tax bill.

Due dates and penalties

Owners who fell behind can ask the office about a delinquent payment contract. Ohio law also permits tax lien certificate sales under section 5721.32 of the Revised Code.

Tax breaks for Miami County homeowners

Almost every program below is filed with the auditor.

How to contest your valuation

Valuation complaints go to the Board of Revision, where the auditor serves as permanent secretary alongside the treasurer and the commissioners' president. Submit DTE Form 1, the Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, to the auditor from January 1 through March 31.

The board then sends a decision or schedules a hearing. A complaint challenges the assessed value and cannot touch the millage rate, which comes from local governments and voters. Build your case with sales of similar homes, photographs or an independent appraisal, which helps but is optional.

Mobile homes and farmland

A mobile home runs on a separate calendar (March 1 and July 31 in the table above). Manufactured home owners register with the auditor, who assesses each home every year and bills it twice. The revenue is shared among townships, cities and schools just as real estate tax is.

Farmland follows another path. The auditor administers the current agricultural use value program, which the Ohio Department of Taxation oversees through soil rate values. In a reappraisal year, applications may be taken all year. Leaving agricultural use can change how land is valued, so talk to the auditor before listing a farm tract.

Transfer fees and selling with taxes owed

The auditor charges $2.00 for each thousand dollars of price, plus 50 cents per parcel for transfer. A check must match the amount to the penny or the conveyance is not processed. Ordinary sales go in on DTE Form 100, and exempt transfers on Form 100 (EX). A fee calculator on the auditor's site gives an estimate.

The recorder, auditor and engineer jointly adopted conveyance standards, and ORC 317.114 has governed recorded documents since July 1, 2009. Before closing, get the tax payoff from the treasurer and ask the closing agent how the current bill is shared. If the buyer will occupy the house, the owner occupancy application is frequently filed with the transfer.

If taxes are past due, the payoff comes out of your sale proceeds at closing. A cash buyer does not change that, though a cash sale can close faster, so request the payoff early and ask the treasurer about any penalty already added.

Which day is the Miami County second installment due?

July 20. The February installment is due on the 14th, and the statement carries exact dates. A payment postmarked by the deadline counts as timely.

How much are late payment penalties in Miami County?

Five percent in the first ten days after the deadline, then 10 percent on unpaid current tax. The treasurer's office offers delinquent payment contracts.

What window applies to a Miami County valuation complaint?

January 1 through March 31, on DTE Form 1 filed with the county auditor. The Board of Revision then rules or schedules a formal hearing.

What fees go with a Miami County deed transfer?

The auditor charges $2.00 per thousand dollars of price and 50 cents per parcel, paid by a check for the exact amount. Use DTE Form 100, or Form 100 (EX) for an exempt transfer.

Where does a Miami County senior apply for the homestead exemption?

Apply at the auditor's office between the first Monday of January and the first Monday of June. Applicants need to be 65 or over, or permanently disabled, and live in the house. Call (937) 440-5925 about the income test.

The offices behind a Montgomery County tax bill

Two offices share the work, both at 451 West Third Street, Dayton, OH 45422. The Auditor sets values and runs appeals, and the Treasurer bills and collects. Reach the Auditor at 937-225-4326. To request the Board of Revision application, call 937-496-6856.

The Treasurer answers at 937-225-4010, weekdays 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Taxpayer Services is Option 1 on that line, and the delinquency specialists are Option 2. The Treasurer also bills a Semi-Annual Property Charge for solid waste services, with questions going to 937-224-8463.

Due dates and penalties

Taxes are billed in two halves. Bills arrive in January and June, and the halves fall due in February and July. In 2026 the dates were February 13 and July 24. A half that goes unpaid past its date draws a 10% penalty.

The county bills a full year in arrears. The first-half bill covers January through June of the prior calendar year, and the second-half bill covers July through December of that year. Manufactured homes are billed in the actual calendar year instead, and their questions go to (937) 225-5255.

  • Paying the full year in February earns no discount. Differences between the halves are assessments, some of which appear only on the first-half bill.
  • If a mortgage servicer pays from escrow, tell them your bill arrived so they can ask the Treasurer for a copy.
  • A prepayment plan spreads taxes across monthly bills for owners with no past-due taxes. Enroll at least 60 days before a half-year due date. Coupons go out at the start of March and August.

The 2026 reappraisal and new values

State law requires a full reappraisal in 2026. The Auditor adjusts values from each property's grade, condition and style and from recent valid sales. The new values take effect at the start of 2027 and show up in bills paid in 2027. They do not change the taxes paid during 2026.

Commercial values are set by use and neighborhood, and apartment, retail and office changes are expected to vary widely. The Property Owner Hotline is 937-224-8927 and Spanish assistance is 937-496-3260. A bigger value does not mean an equally bigger bill, since levies decide the tax rate. The county's own example is a 19% value rise.

How to dispute your value

A complaint to the Auditor's Board of Revision must arrive between early January and March 31. Each complaint is investigated and a formal hearing may follow. Proof falls on the owner, and the board may move a value up or down.

Evidence that tends to help:

  • A record of an open-market sale of the property in the last three years.
  • An appraisal from the last three years.
  • Sales of comparable properties.
  • Photos or repair estimates that document condition problems.

The Auditor counts only valid sales, meaning listings sold on the open market between a willing buyer and a willing seller. Sales between relatives, multi-property sales, sheriff's and bank sales, foreclosure auctions and quit-claim transfers are set aside. Rates move too: a levy that passes can raise a bill, and a property whose value fell can still see a higher bill if the effective tax rate went up.

Homestead reduction

The Homestead Reduction Program serves owners who are 65 or older and owners with a total and permanent disability, and the home must be their primary residence. Call the Auditor at 937-225-4326 with questions about income limits.

A sale triggers one more step. Under ORC 319.202, the buyer's value statement must either affirm that the seller reported no reduction or attach a sworn estimate of the reduction that both sides have accounted for. If you hold a homestead credit, tell your closing agent at the start.

Changing a mailing address or proving what you paid

Address changes for a tax bill must be submitted in writing to the Treasurer, and a Change of Address form is posted for that purpose. If you move out before closing, send it in so the next bill does not go astray.

Payment histories are not mailed automatically. If you pay through mortgage escrow, the amount withheld appears on the 1099 form from the lender. Without records of your own, call 937-225-4010, Option 1, and ask for an itemization of what was paid. To see how a bill is split among schools, townships and other districts, enter your parcel on the Auditor's site and open the Levy Distribution item, or call 937-225-4326.

Late taxes and sold liens

The Treasurer offers delinquent payment plans. An owner who signs a monthly contract pays toward the new taxes while paying off the old ones, without additional interest and penalty. Start at the Treasurer's office or at 937-225-4010, Option 2.

A sold tax lien is different. You cannot make payments on a sold lien through the Treasurer; you arrange payment with the company that bought it. To check release status, look in the Master Information section of the property record on the Treasurer's search page. If it still reads lien sold, the lien has not been released, even if the holder was paid. Title examiners look for that line, so clear it before you list.

Selling a Montgomery County house

Dayton anchors the county, which had 537,309 people at the 2020 census in about 464 square miles. There are near 230,000 parcels and 231,319 households. Owners pay a median of $1,438 a month with a mortgage and $604 without one. The county issued 1,079 building permits in 2025.

Before closing, request the payoff on your parcel from the Treasurer and ask your closing agent how a bill covering a prior year gets split. A cash buyer does not change those steps, but a quick payoff request can speed a short closing.

Because the bill trails by a year, the half you owe at closing may cover time you lived in the house long ago. Expect your closing agent to prorate it, and ask them to show the math in plain terms. If a reappraisal is underway, ask how the new values will affect the buyer's bills in 2027, since that is the question most buyers raise. Keep your bills and receipts together so the title company can match them to the Treasurer's record. If something looks off, call Taxpayer Services before the closing date, not after. That one call can settle a question that would otherwise hold up the sale.

Frequently asked questions

When does the July installment come due in Montgomery County?

The second half falls due in July, and in 2026 the date was July 24. The first half falls due in February, and in 2026 that date was February 13.

What happens if a Montgomery County tax half is late?

A 10% penalty applies to either half left unpaid after its due date.

When is the deadline to dispute a Montgomery County value?

Complaints go to the Board of Revision from early January to March 31. For the new 2026 reappraisal values, the window opens January 1, 2027.

Do I get a discount for paying a whole year of Montgomery County taxes in February?

No. There is no discount for paying the full year at once, and the difference between the two halves comes from assessments.

Can I pay a sold tax lien at the Montgomery County Treasurer?

No. After a lien is sold you deal with the company that bought it, and you confirm the release when the parcel record stops showing lien sold.

Who handles Muskingum County tax bills

Property tax in Zanesville runs through two offices in one building, 401 Main Street. Valuation and relief applications are the auditor's job. Billing and collection belong to the treasurer. After the auditor signs off on a transfer, the recorder files the deed.

Moving the billing address takes a written, signed change-of-address form delivered to the treasurer. Calling in will not do it. A buyer who wants bills mailed elsewhere should send the form right after closing.

How Muskingum County values a house

The auditor appraises each parcel, and Ohio mandates a complete revaluation every six years. The latest rounds were 2018 and 2024. Average values rose 36.135 percent in 2024, a jump that came from three years of climbing sale prices.

A bigger valuation does not mean a bill that grows by the same amount. The bill comes from voter-approved levies, and the Ohio Department of Taxation turns those levies into rates. Next year's rates are not settled before the end of December. An online tax estimator on the auditor's site gives a rough preview, and the auditor's staff can explain how any single value was built.

How to appeal your assessment

Formal complaints are filed at the auditor's office between January 1 and March 31. Under section 5715.19, the true cutoff is March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later. Mailing it is fine: the postal service postmark sets the filing date, while a stamp from a private postage meter carries no weight.

Your case is heard by the Board of Revision, which seats the auditor, the treasurer and a county commissioner, or their stand-ins. Before filing, you can ask the auditor for an informal review. Useful evidence includes:

  • Sales of comparable homes.
  • An independent appraisal from within the past year.
  • Repair estimates for defects in the house.
  • Settlement documents from a recent purchase.
  • Income and expense statements for rentals.
  • Photographs.

While your case is open, the treasurer will accept the lower amount that matches your claimed value. Should the board settle on something higher, interest builds on the shortfall.

Each year brings a winter bill (January or February) and a late-spring bill (May or June), and each shows its own closing date. The statute's default installment dates in section 323.12 are December 31 and June 20, but the treasurer's calendar can differ, so follow the printed date.

A late payment draws a penalty of 10 percent of the current tax, which falls to 5 percent for payments that arrive inside ten days of the deadline. Interest is added to older delinquencies each July 1 and to unpaid current taxes each December 1. Penalties apply even when a bill went astray.

Payment channels: the website portal, the automated line at (833) 505-4134, the kiosk in the lobby, or the Treasurer's Office counter. Expect a fee on electronic payments. Cards are not taken at the window.

Homestead exemption and other relief

Three programs exist, and each one starts with an application at the auditor's office.

  • Owner Occupancy Credit. Takes 2.5 percent off qualifying levies for anyone who owns the home and lives in it as a primary residence.
  • Homestead Exemption. For owners aged 65 and up and for permanently and totally disabled owners. It shields $29,000 of market value for tax year 2025, and income must come in under $41,000. A $58,000 exemption applies to disabled service members and certain surviving spouses.
  • Current Agricultural Use Valuation. Land of at least ten acres in commercial farming is taxed at soil rates. Smaller tracts can qualify with $2,500 of farm income.

Two state bills also matter. House Bill 479 is meant to add roughly $475 of Homestead savings on the bill received in 2027. House Bill 186 set up an Inflation Cap Credit on school levies for tax year 2025. The auditor can tell you how they apply to a given parcel.

Selling with taxes owed

Property tax attaches to the land rather than the owner. The full-year bill goes to the person on title when it is issued, which is why the closing statement gives the buyer a credit covering the months you held the house. Have the title agent show you that proration line before signing.

Unpaid taxes sit on the property as a lien, so whoever buys inherits the debt, and that can stall a deal or lower the price. Once a full year of certified delinquency has run, the prosecutor may begin foreclosure. Foreclosure piles on penalties, interest and court costs and finishes at a sheriff's sale. Muskingum County does not sell tax liens. If you live in the house, the treasurer can write up a delinquency contract that breaks the balance into installments.

Population stood at 86,410 in 2020, with an estimate of 87,014 for 2025. Half of owner-occupied homes are worth more than $182,200, and mortgage holders pay a median $1,300 monthly. A bit under a third of occupied homes are rented, so a sale often involves tenants.

What to do with a new valuation

Search your parcel on the auditor's real estate lookup and note the tentative figure under Values. Compare that number with what comparable houses nearby went for.

If it still seems off, there are two paths. One is the informal review, a conversation with appraisal staff that needs no evidence but rarely changes anything without solid paperwork. The other is the formal complaint to the Board of Revision, which is also where a fresh sale price gets raised.

Each year the filing period ends March 31. Anyone closing in spring should ask whether a complaint is already open on the parcel, since its outcome can alter the bill the buyer ends up with.

Whether taxes rise or fall is not the auditor's call. Voters decide levies, and the state works out rates from those levies and each district's combined value.

Selling for cash

Selling for cash leaves the tax bill intact. What it skips is the lender and the appraisal, which means no financing delays on your closing date. The county treasurer, working from 401 Main Street in Zanesville. Expect one bill in winter and one in late spring.

What is the deadline to contest a valuation?

March 31, with filing opening January 1. State law moves the cutoff later if first-half collection closes after that date.

What is the late penalty?

Ten percent of the tax owed, or five percent when you pay within ten days of the due date. Interest also accrues on delinquent balances.

Who covers property tax at a closing here?

It gets prorated. You credit the buyer on the settlement sheet for your share of the year, and the buyer then pays the actual bill.

Who bills and collects property tax

Both offices that matter are in Ravenna. Values and rates come from the auditor. Bills and payments come from the treasurer, an official elected on a separate ballot. A third body, the Board of Revision, settles value disputes, with the auditor as its secretary and the treasurer among its members.

Choose the office before you dial: the auditor for worth, the treasurer for what you owe.

The auditor's real estate search site, portagecountyauditor.org, offers parcel searches and a tax estimator by taxing district and property value. Look at your own parcel page before listing, because buyers' agents start there.

How a Portage County tax bill is figured

Everything begins with fair market value: the price unrelated parties would agree to on the open market. Ohio assesses 35% of it. That assessed amount is multiplied by the district's total mills and divided by 1,000. All Ohio owners start with 10 mills set by the state constitution. Levies that voters approved for schools, roads, libraries and other services are added to it.

Water line, sewer line and storm water charges are added next, and credits are subtracted last. Rates are recalculated every year, and the treasurer's tax rates page links the published rate sheets for 2010 through the 2025 rates collected in 2026.

  • Mills differ from one taxing district to another, so neighbors in different districts can pay different rates.
  • Special assessments ride on top of the base tax.

One habit worth having before you list: hold the auditor's value up against recent nearby sales, then lay the rate sheet for your district beside your last bill. Spot a mismatch and you can phone the office or file a complaint by March 31.

Call the auditor's office at 330-297-3561 with questions about how rates are calculated, especially if your rate sheet and your bill do not match.

Due dates and penalties

Bills are paid in two halves, one around February and one around July. The July deadline has been known to move. In 2026 the Ohio Tax Commissioner moved the second-half deadline because the new inflation cap credit under House Bill 186 delayed bill processing. The date on your own bill governs, because the state can change a deadline.

Late payment is costly. R.C. 323.121 puts a 10% penalty on a half that goes unpaid past its last date. If the whole amount arrives within ten days after that date, the treasurer cuts the penalty in half. Interest on delinquent balances follows at the statutory rate. An open half at the time of sale comes out of your proceeds. Give the title company notice early.

How to appeal your valuation before you sell

An appeal is possible only during a set window. The auditor takes complaints from January 1 until March 31, and the Board of Revision rules on them. A mailed complaint goes to P.O. Box 1217, Ravenna, OH 44266, and must be there by March 31.

These details commonly trip up owners:

  • Have the DTE 1 complaint signature notarized, or the Board turns it away.
  • Only the current tax year is reviewed.
  • A complaint that relies on a sale must show an arm's length deal. Foreclosure sales, sheriff sales, bank transactions and sales between family members generally do not count.
  • High taxes alone are not grounds, because the Board weighs value, not the bill.
  • Filing does not excuse timely payment. You can pay on your claimed value while the case is open, though any shortfall draws interest.

If the claimed change in assessed value reaches $17,500, the school board may file a counter-complaint within 30 days, and no hearing is set before that. The governing statute is R.C. 5715.19. A second complaint in the same interim period is barred except after an arm's length sale, a casualty loss, a major addition or a 15 percent occupancy swing.

Before recording, a deed goes through the auditor's real estate department. The fee is four dollars per $1,000 of price plus fifty cents a parcel, with form DTE 100 filed. Ohio also lets a county adopt a grantor-paid transfer tax capped at 30 cents per $100 (R.C. 322.02). Ask the auditor whether one is in force on your deed.

For a sale, bring the signed deed, the DTE 100 and a check for the auditor's charge. The treasurer can confirm both halves are paid. Once the transfer is done, the recorder files the deed and, after your lender is paid, the mortgage release.

Portage County housing in brief

Ravenna is the seat of government, and Kent is the biggest city. Population was 161,791 in 2020 on 504 square miles. Owners live in 68.9% of occupied homes and tenants in 31.1%.

Timeline for selling a Portage County house

The tax steps of a sale come in a fairly set order.

  1. Open your parcel on the auditor's site first and read the value, the tax history and any special assessment.
  2. Think the value is too high with March 31 still ahead? Decide whether a notarized DTE 1 is worth filing.
  3. With a signed contract, let the title company know which half of the year's tax you have paid.
  4. If any tax is delinquent, get the treasurer's payoff and forward it to whoever runs the closing.
  5. On closing day the unpaid half comes out of your proceeds, then the auditor transfers the deed and the recorder files it.

Selling with back taxes

Ask the treasurer for a written payoff listing every delinquent year, with penalty and interest, and hand that to the closing agent. Because special assessments stay with the parcel, the auditor can tell you whether any are attached.

  • Print the parcel's tax history from the auditor's real estate site.
  • Find out from the treasurer if a payment plan exists on the parcel.
  • Agree with the title company on who covers the half now accruing.
  • Look for open valuation complaints, since a pending one may alter the amount owed.

If you cannot pay off the debt before listing, a cash buyer can still take the house as it stands, and the tax is paid from the price at closing. Cash Home Buyers CA buys this way and can explain the closing steps.

File form DTE 1 with the auditor at 449 South Meridian Street in Ravenna between January and March. The Board of Revision decides it, and the form's signature must be notarized.

What is the assessed value of a house in Portage County?

35% of fair market value. Your district's mills are applied to that number and the product is divided by 1,000.

Are tax bills paid in two parts?

Yes: roughly half in February and the rest in July. Because the state may move the July date, follow your bill.

What does it cost to transfer a deed?

The auditor's published charge is four dollars per $1,000 of price and fifty cents per parcel. Recording is a separate fee under R.C. 317.32.

Can I sell a house that owes taxes?

Yes. Closing pays it from your proceeds, so request the treasurer's payoff figure before you sign. An as-is contract can be written while the debt is still open.

Who values and who collects

In Richland County one office decides what each parcel is worth (the auditor) and another sends bills and posts the money (the treasurer). Both are in the same Mansfield building, 50 Park Avenue East, ZIP 44902, open weekdays 8am to 4pm. The auditor's number is 419-774-5501 and the treasurer's number is 419-774-5622.

A third body, the Richland County Board of Revision, hears complaints about value. Its three statutory members are the auditor, the treasurer and the chair of the board of county commissioners, and each can appoint a stand-in. Value, exemption and complaint questions belong with the auditor. Balances, payment contracts and delinquency belong with the treasurer.

  • Auditor, 419-774-5501: valuation, Board of Revision complaint forms, owner occupancy and homestead applications, CAUV farmland.
  • Treasurer, 419-774-5622: bills, payments, payment contracts on real estate, and conveyance fee payments.
  • Sheriff's civil section, 419-774-3570: tax foreclosure and bank foreclosure sales.

Richland County housing in numbers

Mansfield is the county seat, and the county has four cities (Mansfield, Ontario, Shelby and part of Galion), villages such as Bellville, Lexington and Shiloh, and 18 townships. Owners live in about 68 of every 100 homes.

When the county revalues property

The county's triennial update falls in tax year 2026, with the resulting bills payable in 2027. Ohio reappraises on a six-year cycle and updates values at the three-year midpoint without a physical inspection.

Three state reforms enacted in late 2025 also affect bills. House Bill 186 adds an inflation cap credit for districts at the 20-mill floor, and where it applies it shows up as a separate line on the bill. House Bill 335 holds inside millage growth to the rate of inflation in reset years. House Bill 129 changes the floor calculation beginning in tax year 2026. None of this ends property tax or freezes values.

How to file a Board of Revision complaint

File the complaint form with the Richland County Auditor, 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. The filing period runs January 2 through March 31, and there is no fee. Section 5715.19 allows filing until March 31 or the end of first-half collection, whichever is later, and counts the mailing postmark.

Call the auditor before filing, because a flawed complaint can be dismissed. Points to remember:

  • One complaint per parcel in a triennial period, unless the property sold, suffered a casualty or lost income. A complaint that was withdrawn still counts as the filing for that period.
  • Parcels can share a form only when they are contiguous or one economic unit, in the same taxing district, with identical ownership. When in doubt, file separately.
  • Attach the supporting documents you plan to use at the hearing when you file.
  • Hearing notice comes by certified mail at least 10 days out, and the hearing takes place in the auditor's office.

If the Board's written opinion still feels wrong, the next stops are the State Board of Tax Appeals and common pleas court.

Evidence the Board accepts

Whoever files carries the burden of proof. Acceptable evidence reads like a checklist: comparable sales, a fee appraisal, itemized repair estimates, the closing statement and purchase contract after a recent sale, and income and expense records for rentals. Outcomes range from an increase to a decrease to no change.

Two limits matter to sellers. Sheriff's sales, bank sales, short sales and any sale where buyer or seller faced unusual pressure are not treated as arm's length, so they do not count as comparables. The Board also has no power over the tax rate, the percentage increase in a bill, the CAUV formula or the dollar amount of a bill, so a complaint that only objects to a higher bill goes nowhere.

Homestead, owner occupancy and CAUV

Three common programs are handled through the auditor. Owner occupancy credit goes to the house you own and use as your main residence on January 1 of the filing year. Homestead exemption reaches owners aged 65 and up, owners with a permanent and total disability, and some surviving spouses. Most face an income test, but service-connected disabled owners do not. Ohio House Bill 96 of 2025 also lets county commissioners adopt a local-option homestead exemption equal to the state amount, which applies without a separate application if the county turns it on. Ask the auditor whether that local option is in place.

Farmland has its own track. Current agricultural use value, or CAUV, lets qualifying land be taxed on its farm value rather than market value. Ohio sets the qualifying bar at ten acres of commercial farming, or a smaller tract earning at least $2,500 a year in gross farm income on average. The formula averages seven years of data with the high and low years dropped.

Farm sellers should note that the buyer's conveyance statement must say whether the land carried CAUV status, and leaving the program can bring a recoupment charge.

Paying the bill and falling behind

Besides real estate, the treasurer takes personal property, mobile home and estate tax, and online card or eCheck payments carry a service fee. Real estate payment contracts exist for prepaying and for catching up. Ohio's default dates are December 31 and June 20, which counties may extend, and your bill shows the dates that apply.

A missed installment draws a ten percent penalty under section 323.121, and half of it is waived when the full amount arrives within ten days. Interest then accrues on delinquent taxes. The delinquent tax collector works with the county prosecutor on foreclosures, which is why an unpaid parcel can move from a bill to a court case.

While a valid delinquent tax contract holds, interest stops, and a breach brings back the interest that was paused. If you hold a contract and plan to sell, get the payoff in writing from the treasurer first.

Tax foreclosure sales

Tax foreclosure sales, when scheduled, are held on Friday mornings at 10:00 in the training room of the Sheriff's Office at 597 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. The sheriff advertises each parcel in a newspaper beginning three weeks before the first sale, reads withdrawals aloud at the start of the sale, and requires the winning bidder to pay in full at the sale. A parcel that draws no sufficient bid can be offered again two weeks later at the same minimum price.

Bank foreclosure sales follow a separate path. To comply with Ohio House Bill 390, they are conducted only online through the sheriff's auction site. The Land Bank, on lower level 1 of the courthouse building, acquires vacant, abandoned houses to reduce blight.

An owner facing a tax judgment should call the treasurer's office at 419-774-5622 before the sale date to ask what payment, contract or sale the county will accept.

Selling when taxes are still owed

Get a written balance from the treasurer, then check it against the auditor's parcel record for the legal description, owner name and mailing address. The buyer's statement filed with the auditor discloses whether a tax reduction or CAUV status applied, and the seller covers the conveyance fee and any county transfer tax before the recorder sees the deed.

Line up three items early: the treasurer's payoff, the auditor's conveyance paperwork and tax map pre-approval for the deed. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, though the payoff and the transfer steps stay the same. Frequently asked questions

Which office answers questions about a tax bill?

The treasurer, at 419-774-5622, answers questions on amounts owed and payment contracts. The auditor, at 419-774-5501, handles value, exemptions and complaints. Both sit at 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield.

When can an owner dispute a valuation?

From January 2 through March 31 each year, filed with the auditor at no charge. The statute lets the deadline run later when first-half collection closes after March 31.

Is 2026 a revaluation year in Richland County?

Yes. The triennial update occurs in tax year 2026, with taxes payable in 2027. State changes from House Bills 186, 335 and 129 are tied to those reset years.

Can selling the house stop a tax foreclosure sale?

Possibly, but ask first. Call the treasurer at 419-774-5622 for the judgment payoff and confirm timing with the sheriff's civil section at 419-774-3570.

Where is a deed recorded after a sale?

With the Richland County Recorder at 50 Park Avenue East in Mansfield. Tax map pre-approval should be included, and documents that need tax map and auditor review must be brought to the courthouse in person.

Ross County at a glance for a home seller

Ross County is hilly, mostly rural Appalachian Ohio, with Chillicothe as its seat and its one city. Beyond the city sit villages including Adelphi, Bainbridge, Clarksburg, Frankfort, Kingston and South Salem, plus 16 townships.

The July 1, 2025 estimate is 76,429 residents and 32,165 housing units. Owners live in 69.6% of homes. An owner-occupied home has a median value of $171,500, and rent runs $906 at the median. With about 112 people per square mile, many parcels are acreage, so a seller with land should ask early whether any of it is taxed under the farm program.

Who values and who bills

Valuation sits with the auditor, and billing and collection sit with the treasurer. The treasurer's office is in the Ross County Courthouse at 2 North Paint Street, Suite F, Chillicothe, Ohio 45601, and the phone is 740-702-3080, the same number given for auditor questions. The email for the treasurer is treasurer@rosscountyohio.gov. The auditor runs an online parcel search and a tax estimator on its own site.

The Board of Revision combines the treasurer, the auditor and the commissioners' president. A complaint is filed at the auditor's office, which passes it to the Board.

Bills reflect values set a year earlier, and the county collects a year behind. Money paid in 2026 settles the 2025 tax year. Ohio requires a full reassessment at least once in six years plus a midpoint update.

Due dates and penalties

Taxes are paid in two halves, with due dates in February and August. A weekend or holiday due date moves to the next business day. Mailings go out in mid-January and again in mid-June or early July. Section 323.12 of the Revised Code names December 31 and June 20 as the baseline, subject to county extension, so call the treasurer's office for the exact days each year.

Ross County penalty and deadline rules

The postmark decides whether a mailed payment is timely, and the treasurer cautions that it often records first processing, which can come after drop-off. Mail early. Anyone whose earlier payment failed to clear must pay by cash, cashier's check or money order.

Tax relief for homeowners

The owner occupancy credit takes a reduction off the home site and the house for owners who live there as a principal residence. Applications are accepted at the auditor's office between January 1 and the first Monday in June. Excluded: rentals, corporate or partnership owners, units inside retail or commercial buildings, depreciation-taxed manufactured homes, and land past the first acre.

The homestead exemption is run through the same office. The Ohio Department of Taxation lists the reduction for a low-income senior or disabled owner at $29,700 of home value for tax year 2026 real property, with an income threshold of $41,000 for that year. The bigger figure, $59,400, covers disabled former service members and widowed spouses of public service officers killed on duty, and carries no income test. The credit equals the tax charged on that slice of value, so a higher local rate means a larger credit. A real property application has to be filed by the last day of the tax year.

  • Penalty remission: request it from the treasurer on Form 23A, and only for reasons Ohio law allows.
  • Military extension: National Guard and reserve members called to active duty, or a spouse or dependent parent applying for them, can get up to five years to pay without penalty or interest.
  • Monthly Budget Pay Plan: a free service that lets owners pay a little each month toward the next bill.

How to dispute your valuation

An owner who disputes the auditor's number files with the auditor's office from January 1 to March 31. If first-half collection ends after March 31, section 5715.19 uses that later day, and mail is dated by postmark. The Board must give ten days' notice of the hearing and decide within 180 days of the filing cutoff.

The treasurer points to the recent sale price, documented by closing papers, as the best proof. A house that has not sold lately needs comparable sales instead, and condition photos can help. The same section limits repeat complaints on one parcel within an interim period. A second filing needs a new event: a sale at arm's length, casualty damage, a big improvement or a 15 percent occupancy swing.

While a complaint is pending, the owner may tender tax computed on the claimed value, and the treasurer is directed to take it.

Options if you owe back taxes

The treasurer offers two plans meant to keep owners out of foreclosure. A Delinquent Tax Contract splits back taxes into five equal installments, with the first due at signing and the rest added to the next four February and July bills. A SMART Payments plan folds current taxes and past-due taxes into one monthly payment that can run 30 months or longer. Under both, no new interest or penalty is added once the contract is signed and the first payment is made, but missing a payment cancels the contract and the stopped charges return. If legal action has already begun, a court cost is added to the first payment.

The auditor publishes the delinquent tax list, so pay or sign a contract by October 31 to stay off it. No fixed date exists by which a property is foreclosed, and the office will work with owners who are struggling.

Recent state changes to property tax

Five property tax bills were signed in late 2025 and early 2026. One changes how sales ratio studies pick the sales used in valuation. One revises the 20-mill floor calculation. One creates an inflation cap credit for school districts at the floor, and every school district in the county sits at the 20-mill floor, with the credit showing up on the second-half bill. One lets county budget commissions trim levies judged unnecessarily high. One caps growth in inside millage at the rate of inflation during reappraisals and triennial updates.

Selling with taxes in play

A tax bill can reach a new owner after closing because the tax follows the parcel. The buyer usually receives a prorated credit in the closing papers, so read the settlement statement closely. Request the balance in writing and ask whether a delinquent tax contract is open. Hand the written figure to the title company so the right amount is held back from your proceeds.

The auditor endorses the deed before recording. The buyer's value statement covers tax reductions and CAUV farm status, and the seller pays the conveyance fee plus any county transfer tax. Under section 322.02 the county rate can reach thirty cents per hundred dollars of value, so ask the Ross County Auditor which rate applies.

A cash sale does not change any of this. The taxes still get prorated, the deed still goes through the auditor, and the title company still needs the treasurer's balance before closing.

Frequently asked questions

When are Ross County property taxes due?

Two payments fall due each year, in February and August. Ask the treasurer at 740-702-3080 for the exact days.

How much is the late charge in Ross County?

Five percent when received within ten calendar days, ten percent after that. Interest on carried-over tax begins August 1, and December 1 applies it to everything past due.

Until when can a Ross County owner contest a valuation?

File at the auditor's office from January 1 through March 31. If first-half collection closes after that, state law extends the window.

Can I avoid the Ross County delinquent tax list?

Yes, by paying or signing a contract with the treasurer by October 31. The payment has to be received, not just postmarked, before the auditor's cutoff.

Which office records the deed after a Ross County sale?

The Ross County Recorder, at 2 North Paint Street, Suite E in Chillicothe, phone 740-702-3000. The auditor must endorse the deed first.

Which Scioto County offices handle property tax

Three county offices share the work, all at 602 7th Street in Portsmouth. The Scioto County Auditor, Room 103 at 740.355.8264, sets values, takes complaints and processes homestead forms. Weekday hours run 8:00 am to 4:30 pm. The Scioto County Treasurer (Room 102, phone (740) 355-8272) sends the bills and collects the money. The Scioto County Recorder, in Room 110, handles the deed last.

The treasurer's office is part of the county's check and balance system with the auditor. In practice that means you ask the auditor why a value changed and ask the treasurer what you owe and when. Both offices are reachable by phone, and the treasurer's website has a Pay Online page for bills.

The latest triennial update

In its latest triennial update, required every three years, the auditor reports an average countywide value increase of about 26.4 percent. State rules require values to stay within 90 to 110 percent of what homes sell for, tested against three years of sales, and strong price gains forced the increase.

Values come from sales data, market trends and statistical analysis, not from a physical inspection of every house. Averages hide big swings between parcels, so check your own record against nearby sales.

Farmland owners should know that current agricultural use value rates are reset in a triennial year by the state, not by the auditor.

The Inflation Cap Credit on your bill

House Bill 186 introduced an "Inflation Cap Credit" for qualifying school district levies. It prints on the bill as a separate line, and parcel-specific inputs make the amount differ from one house to the next.

  • If you paid your second-half bill before the credit was applied, you need not do anything.
  • Any overpayment carries forward and is applied to the next first-half bill.
  • Homeowners who pay through an escrow account at a lender need no action, since the treasurer works directly with lenders.

The state's implementation work delayed the second-half bills in 2026, which shows why you should read the due date on your own bill.

Due dates and late penalties

The statute (R.C. 323.12) allows one payment by December 31 or two installments, the second by June 20. A payment is timely when the treasurer has it by the last day, or when the envelope bears a U.S. Postal Service postmark dated that day or earlier. Postage-meter marks from a private machine are not accepted.

The county can move a date, as it did for the 2026 second half. Always read the due date printed on your bill instead of assuming the statutory one.

How to challenge your property value

The complaint goes to the auditor. R.C. 5715.19 lets you file through March 31 of the next year at a minimum, and longer if first-half collection closes after that date. The auditor hands each filing to the board of revision, and a mailed one is dated by its postmark.

Owners who believe the market value is wrong can file a complaint form with supporting evidence. Good evidence includes:

  • a recent appraisal or closing statement for your own home
  • sales of similar nearby houses
  • repair estimates that show a defect lowering value
  • photos or a report of damage from a casualty

A repeat filing has a limit. Filing twice on one parcel in the same interim period is barred. Four later events lift the bar: an arm's length sale, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement, or occupancy moving by fifteen percent or more.

Homestead exemption

The homestead exemption is a state-funded break for homeowners who reach 65 in the year they first apply, or who are permanently and totally disabled. Applicants must own the house and call it their main residence as of January 1, and stay inside the state's income limits. The auditor offers separate forms for older owners, disabled owners, military service members and the surviving spouse of a public service officer who died on duty.

The applicant's name must be on the deed, and only one application is allowed per property. A reduction, if granted, shows on the bill received the following January. A surviving spouse can qualify between ages 59 and 65 under conditions the auditor can explain. Call 355-8224 or stop in at Room 103 for forms.

Selling with property taxes in mind

Before accepting an offer, get a payoff from the Scioto County Treasurer for the parcel, delinquent balance included. The title company uses that figure to set aside tax money from your proceeds at closing. The deed then goes through the auditor, who endorses the conveyance, and on to the recorder.

A homestead reduction belongs to the qualifying owner, and changes in ownership must be reported to the auditor. The statement of value the buyer files under R.C. 319.202 asks the seller whether the property receives a tax reduction or an agricultural-use valuation. It also carries a notice to the buyer about eligibility for the reduction.

A cash sale follows the same steps. The payoff, the deed endorsement and the recording all happen the same way, so ask for the treasurer's figure first.

If you owe back taxes, call the treasurer before listing and ask whether a delinquent tax contract fits your situation. A valid contract stops new interest while it stays in effect, and the title company can see what balance remains on the parcel. Keep your most recent bill handy at the closing table, since it shows the parcel number and the amounts already paid.

Owner costs in Scioto County

Median monthly owner costs run $1,277 for households with a mortgage and $493 for those without one, and a home's median value is $137,900. Property tax is one piece of those monthly costs, which is why a jump in assessed value is felt even by owners who have paid off their loans. With 28,864 households in the county, ask the auditor's office to confirm what your own parcel receives before you list the house.

Frequently asked questions

When are Scioto County property taxes due?

The statutory dates are December 31 and June 20. The county can move a date, as it did for the 2026 second half, so check the date printed on your own bill.

Who sends the property tax bill in Scioto County?

The treasurer, in Room 102 at 602 7th Street, Portsmouth, phone (740) 355-8272. The auditor sets values; the treasurer mails bills and takes payment.

How long do I have to dispute my Scioto County valuation?

Roughly until the end of March after the tax year; if first-half collection closes later, the window runs to that date instead. Send the complaint to the auditor, and the board of revision rules on it.

What penalty applies if I pay late?

R.C. 323.121 adds 10 percent to an unpaid first half, and another 10 percent to the unpaid current balance once the second-half date passes.

Does the homestead exemption move to the buyer of my house?

No. The break stays with the qualifying owner, and the auditor wants any change in ownership reported. A buyer has to qualify and apply separately.

Canton is the county seat, and the county's 374,853 residents live across seventeen public school districts, from Canton City and Massillon City to Plain Local and Tuslaw Local. Most of a tax bill goes to the schools in the owner's district. A tax rate table for each district is available in print at the Treasurer's office.

Due dates and penalties

Stark County bills in two halves. Statements go out in January for a February deadline and again in June for July. A newspaper notice of the exact day runs about ten days ahead, and the day can shift from year to year.

  • The county gives no personal extensions. A bill turns late the morning after its stated due date.
  • Mailed payments count by the Postal Service postmark. A private meter stamp does not count, and a check dated after the deadline is treated as late.
  • Late current taxes pick up a ten percent penalty, and balances left a full year gather interest.
  • A missing bill changes nothing. Download one from the Treasurer's website, ask for an emailed copy at 330-451-7814, or come to the counter.

The Treasurer also runs a monthly autopay program that lets enrolled owners spread a year's taxes over scheduled draws. Homeowners whose lender pays from escrow still get a courtesy copy each January. If the lender holds the wrong address after a refinance, the lender itself must ask the Treasurer in writing to fix it.

What happens to long-unpaid taxes?

The Treasurer has two tools. A tax lien certificate sale leaves title with the owner but lets the certificate buyer start a foreclosure if the lien stays open. When a parcel is in a lien sale, only full payment in certified funds removes it once letters go out, along with a $200 lien fee. A tax foreclosure, filed through the Prosecutor, ends in a public Sheriff's sale that does transfer title.

The court sequence runs in order. After the complaint reaches the Clerk of Courts, a certified-mail summons gives the owner 28 days to answer. An order of sale then moves to the Sheriff, and a newspaper runs the sale notice for three consecutive weeks. Redemption stays open until the court enters its confirmation, and it requires every tax, assessment, penalty, interest charge, fee and court cost, paid in certified funds.

A seller in this position has a known deadline. Paying the full balance before the confirmation entry is how an owner redeems the parcel, whether the money comes from savings or from a sale.

Back-tax payment plan

Stark County offers plans for delinquent balances only. The Treasurer sets these conditions:

  • The signer must be the titled owner or a documented agent.
  • The delinquent balance has to be at least $1,000. A balance from $1,000 to $1,999 runs 12 months, and $2,000 or more runs 24 months.
  • At signing the owner pays 20 percent of the balance plus the current half.
  • Monthly installments fall on the 20th.
  • An owner who defaulted on an earlier contract cannot sign another.

The current year's bill must still be paid in full and on time, because the office cannot extend a due date or set up a plan for current taxes. Any missed payment defaults the contract. Because a plan is a continuing obligation, a seller should ask the Treasurer for the payoff and settle it at closing.

How do I contest a Stark County valuation?

File a Board of Revision complaint with the Auditor by the March 31 deadline in ORC 5715.19, or by the close of first-half collection if that is later. Keep paying what you believe is due, since the Treasurer may accept the amount figured on your claimed value. The board has 180 days to rule. Some counties run an informal review first, so ask the Stark appraisal department at 330-451-7085 whether one is available. Value is reset by a full reappraisal every six years and an update every three, so check where your parcel sits in that schedule.

Homestead and other tax breaks

The Auditor handles homestead and owner occupancy, the Board of Revision complaint, CAUV for working farmland and exemption or special assessment matters. For tax year 2026 the senior and disabled homestead reduction is $29,700 of market value, with an application due December 31 of the year sought. A denial can be taken to the Board of Revision on form DTE 106B within 60 days.

House Bill 96 of 2025 also lets county commissioners add a local-option homestead exemption. The Homestead department at 330-451-7323 can say whether Stark County has adopted one.

What a seller should check before closing

Ask the Treasurer for the balance on each half, and have the title company confirm the payoff. The Auditor's transfer desk, at 330-451-7333, collects the conveyance fee and applies the stamp the Recorder requires. It charges a rate per dollar of price plus a per-parcel add-on, and it accepts only check or cash.

The Treasurer's site offers real estate search, prior-year search, the delinquent taxpayer list and a page for Sheriff sales. A quick look at your own parcel before listing shows whether anything is open.

Plan the order of events. Taxes are billed in two halves, so the amount a buyer and seller split depends on when in the year the house closes. If you owe back taxes, the payoff comes out of your proceeds at the title company, which is simpler than carrying a plan past the sale. If you cannot clear the balance, a cash sale can close faster than a listing, but the full delinquent amount still has to be paid at settlement.

Frequently asked questions

What is the penalty for paying Stark County property tax late?

Ten percent of the current tax. Interest also builds on balances that sit a full year. The county grants no individual extensions.

When do Stark County property tax bills go out?

January mailings serve the February payment, and June mailings serve July. Exact dates run in the newspaper shortly before each deadline and can move from year to year.

Can I set up a payment plan for Stark County back taxes?

Yes, but only for delinquent balances of $1,000 or more, and only for the titled owner who has not defaulted before. Expect 20 percent down plus the current half at signing, then payments on the 20th. Current-year tax is excluded.

Where do I file a Stark County property value complaint?

At the Stark County Auditor's office, which passes it to the Board of Revision. The board's lines are 330-451-7998 and 330-451-7949, and the state window closes at the end of March the following year.

Does a Stark County tax foreclosure take my house right away?

No. Several steps come first: a court complaint, a 28-day answer period, an order of sale and three weeks of advertising. The owner can still redeem before the court confirms the sale, using certified funds.

Which office to call about real estate taxes

Start with the Summit County Fiscal Office, which houses Auditor, Treasurer and Recorder divisions under a single elected Fiscal Officer. The Auditor division sets values and rates, the Treasurer division issues bills and takes money, and a Board of Revision hears value disputes. County charter creates this one-office setup, and the Fiscal Officer does the work other counties spread across a separate auditor, treasurer and recorder.

The Ohio Building at 175 S. Main St. in Akron is under renovation, which pushed the divisions into temporary quarters, so phone first:

  • Main office: 1-888-388-5613
  • Treasurer: 330-643-2588
  • Real Estate and Appraisal, which handles homestead and assessments: 330-643-2710
  • Board of Revision: 330-926-2559 or bor@summitoh.net
  • Delinquent Tax Department: 330-643-2600

Summit County at a glance

About 538,000 people live in the county, in homes that are mostly owner-occupied (67.5 percent). The median value of those homes is $208,700, renters pay a median $1,026, and median household income is $71,622. Those medians cover the whole county, so any one street may differ. Akron is the seat and largest city.

Seventy-four taxing authorities share the bill: the county, 5 county agencies, 26 school districts, 8 library districts, 14 cities, 8 villages, 9 townships, a water district, a fire district and a recreation district. The two leading digits of a parcel number identify your taxing district, and that district decides the rate.

What goes into a tax bill

Ohio taxes 35 percent of appraised value. The rate stacks up levies that local voters approved. The Fiscal Officer has no power to raise or lower taxes, and the tax rates page links three years of effective rate summaries. Levies come in five kinds:

  • Additional: new money for a taxing body, so bills rise.
  • Renewal: the same yield as an expiring levy.
  • Replacement: swaps in current values for a levy built on old ones, so bills move with the market.
  • Emergency: schools only, a fixed yearly sum over a stated span.
  • Bond: covers principal and interest on a permanent improvement.

The summary of charges on a bill shows the reduction factor, non-business credit, owner-occupancy credit, homestead reduction, current net taxes and current assessments. A bill covers the year before, because Ohio collects one year in arrears. Akron residents with an assessment question call 330-375-2484, and everyone else calls 330-643-2645.

How late can I pay, and what does a miss cost?

Dates print on the bill. There is no grace period, and never receiving a bill is no defense. A missed first half draws a 10 percent penalty. Miss the second half too and the full unpaid current balance, first-half amount included, takes another 10 percent. Under R.C. 323.121(C), paying everything within ten days after a deadline halves that penalty.

Ways to pay:

  • A counter visit to the Treasurer division, checks payable to the Fiscal Officer or Fiscal Office.
  • Mail with a U.S. postmark on or before the deadline. Private meter stamps are rejected.
  • A bank listed on your bill, available only while a collection is open.
  • Phone or web through Official Payments Corporation, which charges 1 percent on debit (minimum $3.95), 2.75 percent on credit (minimum $3.95) or $1.00 per electronic check.
  • Cash at a MoneyGram location, plus a service fee.

Summit also runs a prepayment plan, the Real Estate Discount program. Owners with no delinquency sign up between July 1 and October 31 for a first half, or between January 1 and March 31 for a second half, pay on five of six coupons and earn credit on the early money. Missing the last coupon forfeits the credit.

Disputing a Summit County valuation

Use the Board of Revision, whose window runs from the first of January through the end of March. It rules on value alone and never on the tax amount, and the owner has to prove the claim with paperwork.

Summit County Board of Revision complaints
StepWhat to know
WindowJanuary 1 to March 31
DeliveryMail postmarked by the deadline, a counter visit, or Smartfile online
SeatsFiscal Officer, County Executive, Clerk of Courts, or designees
ProofHanded in, mailed, or uploaded with an online filing
Legal weightFiling starts a legal proceeding

Values are redone every six years, with an update in year three, by comparing a parcel with neighborhood sales. Permits tip off the office to new building. Rewiring, replumbing, framing or foundation work can raise value, while a new roof or routine remodeling does not.

With a complaint pending, R.C. 5715.19 allows you to tender tax computed on your claimed value, with interest on any shortfall if the final number lands higher. Evidence withheld from the board can be excluded on appeal. For storm, fire, flood or demolition damage, file DTE Form 26 by December 31 (damage in the year's first nine months) or by January 31 (last three months).

Homestead and owner-occupancy reductions

The homestead exemption removes the first $29,000 of appraised value on a single-family home from tax, and the office puts average savings at $535 yearly. It covers owners 65 by December 31, the permanently and totally disabled, owners who are rated 100 percent disabled by a service-connected injury, and spouses of first responders who died on duty. The service-connected group sees $58,000 exempted. The 2026 income ceiling for age and disability claims is $41,000, using the owner's and spouse's Ohio adjusted gross income.

The owner-occupancy reduction needs you to own and live in the home on January 1, with the application in by December 31. Rentals are out. It ends when the property transfers, so an incoming owner-occupant files again.

At transfer, R.C. 319.202 has the buyer's conveyance statement confirm that the seller was asked about these reductions. If the house gets one, a sworn note estimating the amount travels with it. Your title company will request the answer.

Back taxes on a Summit County house

The Delinquent Tax Payment Plan, started in 1987, takes owners who missed a half and sets monthly installments. The old balance freezes in a special account with no added interest, leftover interest is abated at completion, and new bills must be paid on time.

The office sells tax certificate liens each late October. Paying in full or entering a plan keeps a lien off that sale. If you would rather sell, ask the title company to request a payoff figure from the Treasurer division and settle it at closing.

Closing is the practical deadline. A buyer's lender will not fund over an open delinquency, so the payoff comes out of your proceeds. Call the Delinquent Tax Department at 330-643-2600 early, before the listing, so you know the number and whether a plan is in place that the buyer must be told about.

Frequently asked questions

What is the late fee on Summit County property tax?

It is 10 percent of the unpaid half. Full payment within ten days after the deadline gets half of that penalty waived under state law.

Can I use the Real Estate Discount program while I owe back taxes?

No. Taxes must be current to enroll. Owners who are behind should ask about the Delinquent Tax Payment Plan.

How soon must I report fire or storm damage to the Fiscal Office?

File DTE Form 26 by December 31 for damage from January through September, or by January 31 of the following year for October through December damage. Send it to appraisedvalue@summitoh.net or mail it in.

Where is my parcel number?

The Fiscal Office property search finds it from a name, address or the number itself. Its first two digits name the taxing district.

Does a postmark on the due date count?

A Postal Service postmark on the due date counts, while a private meter mark does not. Under state law the earliest postmark on the envelope sets the payment date.

Which office does what with your tax bill

Two courthouse-square offices split the work from the second floor of the Administration Building at 160 High Street NW in Warren. The Auditor sets values, takes homestead applications and receives Board of Revision complaints. The Treasurer prints the bills and collects the money.

Rate cards for each taxing district, back to 2010, are linked from the Treasurer's tax information page. Bills, payment history and values live in the Auditor's online property search, except manufactured homes, which are not listed there and need a call to the Treasurer.

Trumbull County has 198,972 people. Owners hold 71.3 percent of occupied homes, the median owner-occupied home is valued at $141,800, and the median rent is $797.

When the county collects and where to pay

Collections come twice a year, usually around March and August, with the exact days printed on each bill. Manufactured homes run on slightly earlier dates. Bills tend to go out by the end of January and again by the end of June. Early payment earns no discount.

Ways to pay:

  • Mail a check or money order to the Treasurer, 160 High Street NW, Floor 2A, Warren, OH 44481. The postmark date is honored.
  • Drop it in the box on Harmon Avenue beside the building's side steps, open around the clock for checks and money orders.
  • Go online through the Auditor's property search and its Tax tab, using an e-check, debit card or credit card.
  • Pay at the counter with cash, check, card or money order.

A processing company charges $1.00 per e-check and 2.5 percent of the total on cards, and the county gets none of it. A returned check costs $15.00. One check may cover several parcels if the parcel numbers are on the memo line. Allow 7 to 10 days after a collection closes for payments to post.

Owners with nothing past due can enroll in the Tax Installment Payment Plan, which prepays through monthly coupons. Ask the Treasurer for a TIP clerk.

How the Auditor values your house

The Auditor runs a mass appraisal for roughly 144,000 parcels: one method, common data, statistical testing. Inputs include field verification, aerial photos, owner-sent settlement statements or appraisals, auction results and listing-service data. Staff generally cannot enter your home, which is a main reason a single bank appraisal can differ. The county compares three years of sales, and the work takes about two and a half years.

The assessed share is 35 percent of market value. Ohio requires a countywide update every three years, and rates then adjust so voted levies raise the same money as before. Only inside millage, 10 mills at most, floats with value. Special assessments for ditches, paving, curbs, sewer and water lines, lighting and trash removal share the bill but are separate from tax.

How do I challenge a Trumbull County valuation?

Go through the Board of Revision, which weighs value and never the tax dollars. State law, R.C. 5715.19, closes the window on March 31 or when first-half collection ends, whichever is later. The person complaining has to prove the case.

MembersAuditor, Treasurer and Commissioners, each free to send a stand-in
