Useful evidence includes an independent appraisal, photos, repair estimates, and a settlement statement with the purchase agreement. A school board can counter-file within 30 days. Taxes stay due during a complaint, and paying in full prevents penalty trouble, with any reduction returned as a credit or refund.

Homestead and other reductions

Three reductions can help a seller or heir:

  • Homestead exemption: up to $29,000 off market value. Owners must be 65 or older, or permanently and totally disabled, or a surviving spouse who was 59 or older when a recipient died. The income cap is $41,000 for 2026 taxes payable in 2027, and $40,000 for a late application on 2025 taxes payable in 2026, using Ohio adjusted gross income for owner and spouse.
  • Disabled-veteran exemption: up to $58,000 for owners rated 100 percent permanently disabled from service, with no income cap.
  • Owner-occupancy reduction: close to 2.5 percent off the bill while the owner lives there, with no filing deadline. It covers the home and one acre.

Appeal a denial on form DTE 106B within 60 days of the notice. Manufactured home owners have until January 31 of the next year. Separately, form DTE 23A asks for remission of a late-payment penalty. The taxpayer files it with the Treasurer, and the board reviews it when the Auditor cannot grant it.

Who owes the tax when a house changes hands?

The owner of record when a bill comes due is responsible, and each bill carries the deeded owner as of the start of the tax year. Sellers and buyers should read their purchase agreement for who reimburses whom. The Treasurer does not keep that agreement, so a title or mortgage company is the place to ask.

At the Auditor's conveyance desk, a transfer costs $4.00 per thousand of value plus $0.50 per parcel, and an exempt transfer costs only the parcel charge. A deed travels to the Tax Map office, then the Auditor, then the Recorder, with a clear copy of the last deed of record. By mail, add a stamped return envelope and a check to the Trumbull County Auditors Office.

Unpaid taxes and foreclosure sales

Tax foreclosure sales are held in person every other Thursday at 1:30 p.m. in the Commissioners' hearing room. Bidding starts at a minimum and rises by $100. The top bidder leaves $3,000 in certified funds and owes the balance 30 days after the sale is confirmed. The owner can redeem until the judge signs that confirmation. Bank mortgage foreclosures have moved to an online site under House Bill 390.

The Trumbull County Land Bank, formed in late 2010 through the Treasurer's office, acquires vacant, tax-delinquent parcels and markets them for reuse, working with Trumbull Neighborhood Partnership. If you would rather sell before things reach that point, ask the title company to request a payoff amount from the Treasurer.

Does Trumbull County count the postmark on a mailed payment?

Yes. The Treasurer honors the postmark date on mailed payments, though posting can take 7 to 10 days after a collection closes.

Can I get a discount for paying the whole Trumbull County bill early?

No. Early full payment earns nothing. Owners who are current can use the monthly coupon plan instead.

Who pays the tax if I sell in the middle of the year?

The owner of record when the bill is due owes it. Your purchase agreement sets who reimburses whom, so read it or ask the title company.

What if the Auditor denies my homestead exemption?

File form DTE 106B with the Board of Revision within 60 days of the denial notice. Manufactured home owners have until January 31 of the following year.

Is there a fee for paying by card?

Yes, 2.5 percent of the total, paid to the processing company. E-checks cost $1.00. Cash, checks and money orders avoid the fee.

Union County offices that handle property tax

Property tax business is concentrated in the County Office Building at 233 West Sixth Street, Marysville, Ohio 43040. Three offices there matter to a seller.

  • Auditor. Sets values, keeps the tax credits, runs the Board of Revision complaint process and stamps deeds. Phone 937-645-3003.
  • Treasurer. Sends bills and collects payment, with a drop box at the rear entrance. Phone 937-645-3035. The office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. and closed on federal holidays.
  • Recorder. Files the deed and any mortgage release after the auditor's stamp. Phone 937-645-3032.

Roughly 70 percent of what the treasurer collects goes to local schools. The county has about 32,800 property records.

How the tax bill is figured

The auditor assigns each parcel a market value. Assessed value is 35 percent of that figure. The assessed value is multiplied by the total tax rate for the parcel's district, and credits then reduce the result.

  • Residential and agricultural property gets a 10 percent credit on net tax for levies passed before November 2013.
  • An owner-occupied home earns an added 2 1/2 percent credit on the house and up to an acre once the owner files form DTE 105C.
  • Levies passed after November 2013 that raise funding carry no rollbacks.

Ohio caps unvoted taxation at ten mills per thousand dollars of assessed value, and any levy above that needs a vote. The county's tax rate page lists rates by district and levy, and the DTE 515 report gives composite reduction factors. To find your own rate, look up the parcel on the auditor's website and follow the “Where your taxes go” link. The first two digits of the parcel number identify the tax district.

If a district line cuts through a house, the school district where the master bedroom sits governs the whole house. That detail can change which schools you can advertise.

Due dates and penalties

Bills are mailed in January and June, and Ohio collects a year behind, so a bill that arrives in 2026 covers tax year 2025. The first half usually falls due in mid-February and the second half in mid-July or August. The treasurer announces exact dates each year.

Union County late-payment charges
Payment stageWhen it appliesPenalty or interest
First half unpaidDay after the due date, then ten days later5 percent, then 10 percent
Second half unpaidDay after the due date, then ten days later5 percent, then 10 percent
Prior years' delinquencyEach September 14.67 percent interest
Total unpaid balanceEach December 12.33 percent interest

For mailed checks, the postal cancellation date controls. A stamp from a private postage meter does not count. A missing bill never excuses a late payment, so call the treasurer if yours does not show up.

Paying the bill or spreading it out

Send checks to the Union County Treasurer at the Sixth Street address by mail, in person or in the back drop box. Cards and e-checks work online, and a processing fee goes to the payment vendor instead of the county. Some years the treasurer also takes payments at a Richwood bank on set days before each due date, so check the payment information page for any such location.

Two programs help with budgeting:

  • Real Estate Tax Escrow Program. Prepay by the month, and the treasurer applies the funds as each half comes due.
  • Delinquent payment plan. A written contract with the treasurer lets you pay back taxes in installments while keeping current tax paid. Penalty and interest are held in escrow and removed once the contract is paid off, and added back if you default.

Unpaid bills draw a delinquent notice in late September or early October, and the owner's name is printed in the paper's delinquent list. When tax is still owed the following November, the file goes to the county prosecutor to begin foreclosure.

Appealing your valuation

The auditor receives each complaint and passes it to the Board of Revision. State law sets the cutoff in Ohio Revised Code 5715.19: March 31, or the day first-half collection closes if that is later.

  • File a notarized DTE Form 1 by email, fax or mail to the Auditor's Office, Attn: Board of Revision, at the Sixth Street address.
  • Contest the current tax year only. The board does not look back.
  • If you bought or sold recently, attach the closing statement, purchase contract, escrow statement and deed.
  • Hearing dates follow the order in which complaints arrive.
  • A business or trust should use an attorney. An individual does not need one.

If the change you want tops $50,000 in market value (or $17,500 assessed), the school board is notified. Decisions are held for 30 days, and a refund or credit follows about sixty days after that. You have 30 days from the decision letter to appeal, either to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals on DTE Form 4 or to the Court of Common Pleas. A decision often holds until the next triennial update. The last full reappraisal was in 2019, with updates every third year after.

Homestead exemption and CAUV

The auditor runs two programs that a buyer or seller may ask about.

  • Homestead Exemption. Open to owners age 65 or older, owners who are permanently disabled, and a surviving spouse aged 59 to 64 of someone already receiving it. The applicant must own the house and live in it, and the filing cutoff is the first Monday in June. Owners with a military service disability use form DTE 105I. Call the auditor for the current income cap.
  • Current Agricultural Use Value (CAUV). Land of at least ten acres worked commercially for three years can be taxed on what it earns as farmland. A parcel under ten acres needs $2,500 average yearly gross income. Applications count only if the auditor's office has them in hand between the January and March dates, whatever the postmark says. Leaving the program triggers a charge equal to the previous three years of tax savings.

When a property sells, section 319.202 asks the grantee to confirm whether the seller said the property carried a rollback or CAUV status. If you own CAUV land, talk to the auditor before closing about the recoupment charge.

Selling with taxes owed or due

The settlement statement normally prorates the tax by date, and that ends your responsibility for later bills. If a bill still reaches your mailbox after the sale, hand it to the new owner or phone the treasurer so a corrected bill can go out. Read the settlement statement closely, because a bill for the prior year can come due after you have moved.

Here is how to handle it step by step.

  • Ask the title company to search for delinquent tax before you list.
  • If back taxes show up, the delinquent payment plan can cover them, or the title company can pay them from your proceeds at closing.
  • Ask the treasurer for the rate sheet covering your district so you can tell buyers what the carrying cost looks like.

Warren County offices that handle property tax

Two elected offices split the work. The Warren County Auditor values property and administers credits. The Warren County Treasurer sends the bills and takes payment. The auditor's office is at 406 Justice Drive in Lebanon, and its real estate department answers at 513-695-1235.

The auditor keeps records on about 91,400 parcels, covering ownership, legal description, property address, building description, appraised value and the transfer history that feeds the tax list. The treasurer posts rate sheets for every year from 2004 through 2025, so you can look up how your parcel's levies have moved.

Complaints about value go to the Board of Revision, a panel of three that seats the auditor, the treasurer and the commissioners' president.

How the county values a house

Each parcel is appraised at estimated fair market value and taxed at 35 percent of it, which is Ohio's common level of assessment. A general reappraisal includes a site visit to every parcel at least once every six years. A triennial update adjusts values in the third year between those cycles, usually by percentage changes drawn from local sales.

New construction and changes in use are valued every year. The tax lien date is January 1, so ownership and use on that day fix the bill payable the following year.

Most increases follow the state-required reappraisal, and without new construction or new levies, bills tend to stay near the same level between updates. A school levy passed by voters in a district raises bills for the parcels inside it, which is why two similar homes in different school districts can pay different amounts.

Due dates and how to pay

Ohio real estate tax is billed in two halves, with the first half due in February and the second half in the summer. The treasurer announces exact dates each year. In years when the state delays the second-half bills, wait for the bill instead of sending an estimate.

You can pay through the myWarrenCountyOhio portal, by calling 513-496-2931, or in person weekdays between 7:30 am and 4:30 pm. The treasurer's page posts these forms:

  • Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties.
  • Military Extension Application.
  • Notice of Possible Tax Adjustment.

Late charges come from Revised Code 323.121. An unpaid half draws a ten percent penalty, cut in half when the whole amount arrives within ten days of the deadline. Delinquent balances also collect interest at the rate set under section 5703.47.

If you believe the auditor's value is too high, form DTE 1 is the tool. The auditor accepts it from January 1 through March 31 of the next tax year, and a notary must witness the signature of the owner or the owner's attorney.

The board decides market value for land and buildings together, never the tax dollars or rates. The owner carries the burden of proof, so a weak case can leave the value alone or even push it up. The board sends notice at least ten days before the recorded hearing and later mails or emails a decision letter to each party.

  • Good evidence includes a recent sale for less than the county's value, a recent fee appraisal, and proof of damage or defects that hurt the home's worth.
  • The board may also request purchase or lease agreements, closing statements, construction cost records, rent rolls and income and expense statements.
  • Get supporting papers to the board before the hearing date.

The share granted depends on the quarter: 100 percent for January to March, 75 for April to June, 50 for July to September and 25 for October to December. Farmland in the CAUV program is valued on expected farm income. It is open to farms over 10 acres in commercial use for three years and to smaller ones grossing at least $2,500 a year, with a $25 first-time filing fee and a payback of up to three years of savings if the use changes.

What changes on the tax side at a sale

A yes means a sworn paper estimating the reduction or the recoupment, signed by buyer and seller. The statement also reminds the buyer to tell the auditor if the home later stops qualifying for the reduction.

One more Ohio rule applies to landlords. When the house is residential rental property, the auditor's endorsement on the deed tells the new owner to file rental registration information.

Before listing, ask the treasurer for a written payoff covering penalties and interest. The title company will want it for the closing statement. The Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties is the way to ask for relief on penalties.

The county also runs forfeited land sales for parcels with long unpaid balances. Ask either office how a delinquent parcel moves toward that kind of sale, and settle the balance early.

  • Get the payoff figure from the treasurer.

The Warren County Treasurer does. The auditor sets the value, and the treasurer bills, collects and posts rate sheets. You can pay through myWarrenCountyOhio or by phone at 513-496-2931.

Thirty-five percent of appraised value is the taxable value. The auditor reappraises every parcel at least once in six years and updates values in the third year between.

March 31 closes the window. A DTE 1 complaint can go to the auditor starting January 1 of the following tax year, and the signature has to be notarized.

For the 2026 tax year the limit was $41,000 of 2025 Ohio adjusted gross income. You must be 65, permanently disabled, or a surviving spouse who is at least 59, and the application must reach the auditor by December 31.

Can I get Warren County late-payment penalties removed?

You can apply. The treasurer posts an Application for Remission of Late Payment Penalties and a Military Extension Application. Under Ohio law, paying the full amount within ten days of the due date also cuts the penalty in half.

What the 2026 triennial update did to home values

Residential values rose 19 percent on average countywide. The state runs a full reappraisal every sixth year with an update in between. The county did its reappraisal in 2023, which made 2026 the mid-cycle adjustment.
